People who can't use a mouse or trackpad, often (if not always) navigate by using their keyboard. You can experience this yourself by using the tab-key and your arrow-keys. You might notice that although the order on most pages of the platform is correct, you often can't actually see where you are. Some browsers indicate this better than other browsers do, but there are many buttons/links that do not have any indication that they're ''highlighted''.

## Description

The goal is to have referential integrity in our database, have all relations properly defined and to have the SQL / migrations match the typeORM entities. That way we'll decrease number of data-related bugs, amount of redundant / orphant data in database and thus increase performance. As an additional benefit, we may be able to reduce the codebase.

## Initiative / goal

This initiative / epic will make the application more stable and will reduce user misery.

### Hypothesis

The hypothesis is that there is a large number of known and also a large number of unknown issues related to data integrity. We have hit many issues in the space of:

- storage buckets
- storage aggregators
- callouts
- profile
- journeys

Frequently aggregating queries in the business logic querying multiple entities should build / be part of a tree of dependencies. When a part of that tree has missing relationships the whole logic is broken and we do a lot of patching to fix it, show / no show errors and end up bypassing the root cause of the problem.

Additionally, with a lot of extra rows of the database, that increases its capacity --> cost + reduces the speed of query execution in the tables with orphan data.

Missing relationships on database level also prevent automation / scripting to have a generic solution created for iterating over all the relationships and cleaning up orphaned data.

Performance gain is expected, depending on the size of the orphaned. Mostly on Read due to the indexes.

## Acceptance criteria and must have scope

- [ ] Database schema defined in a way that the database integrity check can be enforced
- [ ] Indexes added
- [ ] Orphaned data cleaned up
- [ ] Ability to run orphaned data clean up manually on a periodic
- [ ] TypeORM definitions to match the database schema
- [ ] Able to generate schema migrations automatically

## Stakeholders

Dev team.

QA

## Timeline

Target: Q1 2024

## Design

## Objective
This document outlines the current plan for stress testing the multi-user Whiteboard feature and the findings along the way. The primary goal is to share all the findings and use them to build a plan to move forward.

## Prerequisites
1. Space
2. The Space to be able to host Multiuser Whiteboards (license/flags)
3. A predetermined amount of registered users per scenario
4. Users assigned as members of the Space OR users with elevated access with UPDATE access to the Whiteboards
5. A predetermined amount of Whiteboard posts per scenario

## Gaps (addressing Prerequisites)
1. There is base scenario that creates the an Organization with Account and assigns a Space to it.
It also requires many users with different credentials to be created as part of the base scenario, which is not a requirement for the stress test.
In addition, to register them properly it requires a mailslurper which is not available on all environments
2. Doable (Either reuse existing code or write new)
3. Requires a mailslurper
4. Doable (Either reuse existing code or write new)
5. Doable (Code is written)

### Extra gaps
- ?

## Current setup
1. Most of the gaps are circumvented by manually creating a Space and Callouts and having the Whiteboard IDs hardcoded into the test.
2. No users are registered but the Space's privacy is set to **Public** which makes the Whiteboards readable.
3. A temporary version of the whiteboard service is deployed which allows all users with read access to also be able to update

## Additional considerations
- Increased memory overhead per connected socket (user)
- Increased memory consumption related to messages being buffered

### Multi-instanced microservice setup
- A working hypothesis is that a multi-instanced setup would reduce the memory footprint and offload the CPU versus a single-instanced setup. A careful think through is needed to consider all the scenarios and the targeted behaviour.
Some of the considerations include:
- where will the state be calculated
- is every instance calculating the instance on it's own or it's at a round-robin principle

### Improvements
- **Offloading the heavy lifting of the state reconciliation to a separate worker thread**
- Redis or a durable queue to offload the memory pressure off the microservice
- Throttle client sends: clients are throttled if the current server load is high

## Description
The current usage of organizations causes a lot of confusion:
- Profiles suggest huge organizations are partnering with Alkemio, when actually there are just very specific teams or departments working on Alkemio
- Unclarity about who is 'behind' an organization profile
- Organization profiles used to affiliate organizations with a specific challenge are a kind of 'dead' profiles, but it still seems like you can send them an email etc

There are a couple of needs when in comes to organization profiles:
- Clarity on who is 'behind' it
- See where this org is participating in
- See if it is 'real' and alive.
 
The envisioned solution is to make a clear split between Verified and Unverified organizations, plus splitting the Organization name from the Department/team etc, in which the Department/team gets the profile page, and the organization is simply a sort of tag on this profile. Clicking on this tag would then allow the user to see all profiles associated to this organization, and all the spaces these profiles are participating in.

Verified organizations
- Team/Department name
- Organization
- Bio, full profile, like it is now
- Contact person
- Send a message
- Profile visible outside of the Spaces, eg on Contributors page, later maybe in Recommended sections

Unverified organization
- Team/Department name
- Organization
- No additional profile info
- No contact person
- Not able to send a message
- Profile card only visible from within the Space/Search
- Clear indication that this profile is not 'verified' (maybe use different name), plus button to verify

## Goal
Clarity for users, proper way of indicating affiliated organizations when they are not actually active on the platform

## Hypothesis
Better usage of organization profiles, overall richer impression when exploring, less frustration of users,

## Must have scope
- [ ] 'Name' of former org profile to be more specific
- [ ] New name for Organization profile? Maybe something like Team profile?
- [ ] Organization to be more of a label/tag, not a profile
- [ ] Page to see all profiles + journeys related to an organization
- [ ] Unverified profiles to have a completely stripped down version, see details in description above

## Description
Organizations currently get associated with both Spaces and Users through direct admin action rather than a consent-based flow, mirroring a gap in how the platform already treats individual users. Today, a lot of this still depends on the Alkemio team manually creating and adding organizations on behalf of others — there's no self-serve way for a Space or an org admin to bring an org in themselves.

This Epic covers two symmetric flows that remove that dependency and share the same invitation pattern (merged from #1479, which is being closed as a duplicate of this epic):
1. **Org → Space**: a Space admin invites an organization to join, instead of it being added directly.
2. **User → Org**: an org admin invites a user to associate with the organization, instead of adding them directly.

Both reuse the invite/accept-decline dialog, notification pattern, and RoleSet infrastructure already built for Space community invitations.

## Goal
Make the role of organizations on the platform easier to use — reducing friction and confusion in how orgs get associated with Spaces and Users, by replacing unconsented direct-add actions with a clear, consistent invite/accept flow.

## Hypothesis

b: ## Description Two long-running epics on this backlog were really two mechanisms for the same thing: helping a community surface, structure and learn from what it collectively knows and believes. This epic merges them. - **Polis** — anonymous statement / agree–disagree–pass clustering. Optimised for *breadth*: getting a signal out of a large, loosely-engaged crowd, quickly, with no onboarding. - **Choral Explanations** (merged in from #936) — attributed, long-form, many-voices answers to a shared question, Stack Overflow style. Optimised for *depth*: building shared understanding from named people writing in their own voice. Reference: https://hapgood.us/2016/05/13/choral-explanations/ They are opposites on nearly every axis that matters — anonymous vs. attributed, one click vs. an essay, crowd vs. committed community, statistical vs. editorial — and that is precisely why they belong in one discussion rather than two. The question this epic exists to answer is not "which of these do we build", but: **what is Alkemio's model of collective intelligence, and which mechanism serves which moment in a community's life?** A plausible answer is that they are sequential rather than competing — Polis to find out where a crowd actually stands, Choral Explanations to have the committed community work through what to do about it — but that is the thing to decide, not an assumption. ## Goal Usage of Alkemio. Compelling functionality on Alkemio. Surfacing and learning from the collective wisdom of a community is core to making progress, and to having an engaged community that finds real value in collaborating here. ## Hypothesis ### On Polis Polis is a very well known tool in certain public interest communities. - It can be an interesting additional feature for existing Alkemio communities. It is an advanced way to gather insights from a community by proposing statements, allowing the community to respond, and analysing the (changing) results. - Integrating Polis into Alkemio would not necessarily bring existing Polis users over to Alkemio. They use Polis because of its main value: super easy to use, very simple interface, and can be done anonymously. Alkemio will add too much complexity if they are looking for that simplicity. - For those working *with the outcomes* of Polis, Alkemio is very powerful. Imagine working on your initiative in a Space, sending a Polis link to citizens to easily gather insights, and analysing those insights in the Space. But it is the admins looking at the outcomes in the Space — not the citizens being onboarded into a Space to give simple feedback. - We can always test iFrames with Polis, to see whether our users are interested and what the use case is. ### On Choral Explanations A Q&A format has a much lower barrier to entry than a greenfield wiki or a document management system. The modality encourages community members to engage personally, in their own voice, and potentially across multiple media (markdown, documents, video). Surfacing the collective wisdom of a community this way is key to an engaged community that finds value in the collaboration. ## Must have scope ### Framing (do this first) - [ ] Decide Alkemio's position on collective intelligence: which mechanism serves which moment, and whether they are sequential, parallel, or one is out of scope - [ ] Decide where the outputs of either mechanism land in the domain model — is a Polis result an artefact in a Space? Is a "choral" question a callout type? ### Polis - [x] For now, explore usage of Polis via iFrames - [ ] Investigate why Polis sign-in does not work through an iFrame — may be structural, and good to know either way - [ ] Later, further integration ### Choral Explanations - [x] Comments on Callouts - [x] Add liking / reactions to contributions - [ ] Different layout for the cards - [ ] Filtering of Callouts as they scale - [ ] Vote a contribution up **or down** — anonymity is needed for votes to be useful - [ ] Easy way to link to other contributions, e.g. searching for contributions in the Space to link to, the way GitHub issues link to each other ## Open partner feedback carried over from #936 These items were raised by TIP against the Knowledge Base and were still open when #936 was closed. They are carried here so they are not lost. Several are Knowledge Base UX rather than collective intelligence proper, and may deserve their own issue — flagging rather than silently dropping. - `2022-12-003` Edit callout answers **while keeping version history**, ideally with a group authorised to edit others' answers - `2022-12-004` Card preview title truncated to a single line — making the title optional would be better still - `2022-12-007` ⚠️ **Explicit Creative Commons license per callout / callout response** (CC BY 4.0 or CC0 1.0), made explicit in the submission form. Raised repeatedly; the proposed tagging solution was assessed as not solving it. Blocks reuse of the knowledge base. - `2022-12-008` Up **and down** voting on contributions, with anonymity. Emoji reactions are a partial first step only — see #1866 - `2023-06-002` Clarify the Knowledge Base start page (cf. stackoverflow.com/questions) - `2023-06-003` Merge Q&A into one integrated page — 1 question, multiple answers, small comments per Q/A - `2023-06-004` Ability to add instructions or limit options in the callout/answer creation workflow - `2023-06-005` Ability to add instructions at the top left of the Knowledge Base - `2023-06-006` ⚠️ **Link to a question or answer without having to define the link title statically.** Not fixed, not planned. Makes it hard for users to reuse knowledge in their own contributions. - `2023-06-012` Switch between NL and EN in contributions, ideally with inline translation. Called out as blocking expansion of the TIP community to non-NL contributors. ## Stakeholders ## Design Figma file: _Comments are highly appreciated. When commenting in Figma, please also leave a note in the comments box below this issue to notify us_ Sub-issue: #937 — Design for Choral Explanations ## Additional context ### Polis See https://alkem.io/demodemo/challenges/coordination-5385 > Community Building tab, and https://alkem.io/demodemo/challenges/coordination-5385/collaboration/communityfeedback for an example of how the polls look embedded in a post via an iFrame. A second post uses an iFrame for the moderation part, but sign-in does not appear to work through the iFrame at the moment. Polis is an app that enables open and positive dialogue between people with different opinions on complex topics. Using machine learning and human interaction, Polis helps groups understand each other and find common ground. It can be used for group decision-making, public involvement and public opinion research. - https://polispilot.nl/ · https://gitlab.com/betabreak/polispilot — a fork of https://github.com/compdemocracy/polis - https://polisnl.org/ · #polisnl via https://praatmee.codefor.nl/ PolisNL is a 'layer' on top of old Polis (2013 — very outdated design, not compliant with privacy regulations, difficult codebase). Their key criteria are: explainable, traceable, reliable. A new version was due early Feb 2025: more user friendly, 3 visualisations of the answers, personal branding, embedding in a website. Answers (yes/no/skip) are not customisable for now. Conference 9–10 Oct on Digital Democracy. ### Merge record - Merged in: #936 (Choral Explanations, opened Jan 2023, closed 25 Aug 2026) - Sub-issue #937 re-parented from #936 to this epic
t: Collective intelligence: Polis + Choral Explanations

## Phases Overview

### Phase 1 — Apollo 5 + NestJS 11 (this epic)
Upgrade the core framework and GraphQL stack. Can be done together since `@nestjs/apollo@13.x` bridges both.

### Phase 2 — Node 24 (this epic)
Upgrade the runtime to Node.js 24 LTS after Phase 1 stabilizes.

### Phase 3 — ESM Migration (separate epic, deferred to NestJS 12 ~Q3 2026)
Migrate from CommonJS to ESM once NestJS 12 ships native support.

---

## Description
This Epic covers upgrading the server technology stack to current versions. **Apollo Server 4 reached end-of-life on January 26, 2026.** NestJS 11 is the current stable release. Node 24 is the current LTS.

Since we have more than a few services using NestJS but they are fairly isolated and can work independently, we should approach it on a service-by-service basis.

### The primary job to be done is:
- As a backend engineer, I want to upgrade to NestJS 11, Apollo 5, and Node 24 so that we can leverage performance improvements, new features, and long-term support.

### Secondary:
- As a product team, we want to ensure that platform reliability and maintainability are upheld during framework upgrades.

## Phase 1 — Apollo 5 + NestJS 11

- Upgrade `@nestjs/*` from 10.x → 11.x
- Upgrade `@nestjs/graphql` + `@nestjs/apollo` from 12.x → 13.x
- Upgrade `@apollo/server` from 4.x → 5.x
- Upgrade `graphql` to >=16.11.0
- Handle Express v5 as new default — route matching changed (`?`, `*`, `+` require named params)
- Keep `graphql-upload@13` (CJS-compatible) or switch to `graphql-upload-ts`
- Verify `graphql-amqp-subscriptions`, `graphql-ws`, custom APM Apollo plugin compatibility

**Key findings:**
- Apollo 5 ships both ESM + CJS — **no ESM migration required**
- Express integration extracted to `@as-integrations/express4` or `@as-integrations/express5`
- `status400ForVariableCoercionErrors` now defaults to `true`
- Plugins use Node.js built-in `fetch` instead of `node-fetch`
- NestJS 11: Express v5 is the new default, middleware registration order changed (global modules first), CacheModule updated
- NestJS 11 does NOT require ESM

## Phase 2 — Node 24

- Update Dockerfile base image, Volta pin, engines field
- Test Undici 7 / stricter `fetch` behavior
- Verify all native modules compile
- Test AMQP/RabbitMQ connections under new Node version

## Current State (server repo)

| Component | Current Version | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Node.js | 22.21.1 | 24 LTS |
| NestJS | 10.3.10 | 11.x |
| @apollo/server | 4.10.4 | 5.x |
| @nestjs/graphql | 12.2.0 | 13.x |
| @nestjs/apollo | 12.2.0 | 13.x |
| TypeScript | 5.3.3 | 5.x (latest) |
| graphql | 16.9.0 | >=16.11.0 |
| graphql-upload | 13.0.0 | 13 or graphql-upload-ts |
| TypeORM | custom fork | custom fork |

## Risk Areas

| Area | Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| `graphql-upload@13` | Old, but CJS-compatible | Switch to `graphql-upload-ts` for dual CJS+ESM support |
| Express v5 route matching | Route patterns may silently change behavior | Audit all routes + global prefix |
| TypeORM custom fork | May need rebasing for NestJS 11 | Test thoroughly |
| `graphql-amqp-subscriptions` | Small package, may not track Apollo 5 | Verify compatibility |
| Custom APM Apollo Plugin | Verify Apollo 5 plugin API | Check `ApmApolloPlugin` |

## Success Metrics
- All services build and deploy successfully post-upgrade
- Test suites pass with no regressions
- Engineering team feedback is positive on working with the upgraded version
- No production issues arise from the upgrade within two weeks post-release

## Must Have Scope
- Audit dependencies and their compatibility with NestJS 11
- Audit the current CI/CD pipelines for potential impact (Travis, Docker)
- Refactor breaking changes introduced in v11 (e.g., GraphQL updates, package reorganizations)
- Run and pass all existing unit and integration tests
- Document any relevant migration details and lessons learned
- Smoke testing of major services and GraphQL APIs

## Stakeholders
- Engineering – core backend team (responsible for implementation)
- DevOps – ensure build & deployment remains stable
- Product – for awareness of possible temporary slowdowns in feature delivery
- QA – to validate stability and regression coverage
- Community – in case any user-facing issues arise that need explanation
t: Phase 1 & 2: NestJS 11, Apollo 5, Node 24

## **Description**

Scale up Alkemio’s Matrix-based communication infrastructure by deploying and configuring Synapse with horizontally scalable architecture. 


---

## **Goal**

Support the business initiative of enabling community-driven, cross-organizational collaboration by scaling from tens to hundreds of concurrent workspaces and thousands of users without performance degradation.

---

## **Hypothesis**

If Synapse is implemented using a horizontally scaled, worker-based setup (with Redis and PostgreSQL), then:

* **Performance targets**:

  * Average `/sync` latency < 200 ms
  * Error rates < 5% under 2,000 concurrent users
* **Leading indicators**:

  * `/sync` latency metrics
  * CPU/RAM usage of worker processes
  * Depth of Redis queue backlog
  * User‑reported issues from pilot workspace

---

## **Must-have scope**

**In-scope for launch**:

1. Synapse deployed in a horizontally-scalable setup.
2. Redis for pub/sub replication and caching.
3. Tuned PostgreSQL for high-volume event throughput.
4. Basic client support: group rooms, room tagging, message threading.
5. Monitoring dashboards (latency, CPU/RAM, Redis queue).
6. Pilot test in a high-concurrency workspace (≥ 500 users).

**Out-of-scope (for later epics)**:

* Voice/video calls
* Bot integrations
* Advanced moderation via policy servers

---

## **Stakeholders**

* Product Team
* CTO
* Engineering Team

---

* Synapse can scale across multiple Python worker processes tackling `/sync` and other streams ([element.io][1], [matrix.org][2], [matrix.org][3], [matrix-org.github.io][4], [reddit.com][5], [matrix-org.github.io][6])
* Official documentation outlines Redis-based replication, multiple worker processes, and deployment steps 


---

## Description
This Epic serves as a bucket for tracking operating system (OS) and browser-specific issues that are low-priority due to minimal usage. These issues may only appear on niche or outdated OS/browser versions that are rarely used by our customer base. While we do not prioritize fixing these immediately, we want to keep them documented for future reference, potential fixes, or if usage patterns change.

## Goal
The goal of this Epic is to maintain visibility and documentation of OS/browser-specific issues without diverting resources from higher-priority work. This ensures we can revisit these issues if they become more relevant (e.g., increased usage of a previously niche OS/browser).

## Hypothesis
We hypothesize that tracking these issues will:
- Reduce duplicate reports by having a centralized location for known edge cases.
- Allow us to quickly address issues if they become more widespread.
- Improve transparency with stakeholders (e.g., Customer Support) when users encounter these problems.

## Must-Have Scope
- A centralized list of documented OS/browser-specific issues.
- Clear labeling of affected platforms (e.g., "Windows 7 + Firefox ESR").
- Basic triage notes (e.g., reproduction steps, severity, and potential workarounds).
- Regular reviews (e.g., quarterly) to reassess prioritization based on usage data.

## Stakeholders
- **Engineering Team:** Responsible for triaging and documenting issues.
- **Product Team:** Decides if/when to prioritize fixes based on business impact.
- **Customer Success/Support:** References this Epic when users report issues on unsupported platforms.
- **QA Team:** Helps verify and document reproduction steps.


**Additional Notes:**
- This Epic is not tied to a specific release timeline.
- Issues here may be revisited if usage data or customer feedback indicates a need for action.

## Description
The metric is clear on individual contributions where you create a single contribution, e.g. a Post was published - one contribution is counted per contributor on that resource.
It gets trickier for multi-user contributions where the contributions were part of a joint session, e.g. Whiteboards, Memos.

Current behaviour of Whiteboards:
- When the time window finishes, ONLY the active users are checked for contributions
- When the session is closed, no contributions are registered.

Current behaviour of Memos:
- When the time window finishes, ALL the contributions made over time are registered
- When the session is closed, ALL contributions are registered. **This opens a window for abuse, where you can open and close multiple sessions with a single contribution and register many contributions in a minute.**

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The defined behaviour is changed in the Whiteboards and Memos
- [ ] A timer is started with the start of the session - the resource is loaded for the first time
- [ ] While the time is running, contributions are gathered
- [ ] After a fixed amount of time, per configuration, ALL the contributions created over time are gathered, and one event is created per User per the resource.
- [ ] A single contribution is counted when:
  - if the user was disconnected, but made a contribution
  - if the user has entered multiple times over time and made multiple contributions
  - if the user has multiple sessions opened of the same resource and made at least one contribution across all sessions
  -  If the session is closed before the window runs out, no matter how short it was

## Additional Context
- A session is considered cut short if it was closed between the end and the start of the time window
t: More accurate North Star Metric tracking (TE:3)

## Description
This epic focuses on the development of an automated end-to-end test suite for the core functionality of our React/TypeScript client. The goal is to move critical regression tests from manual execution to an automated process to achieve faster feedback on code changes. The automation will specifically target the client's interaction with the backend through GraphQL and Apollo.

## Goal
To establish a highly efficient, maintainable, and fast-running client automation framework that can validate core functionality of the application. The new suite must provide rapid feedback to the development team, integrate seamlessly into our CI/CD pipeline, and support parallel execution to minimize total run time. The ultimate aim is to reduce manual regression effort and increase deployment confidence.

## Short-term goal
Have a framework that can authenticate different users on different browsers.

## Hypothesis
By automating the core regression test cases and optimizing data setup via the API, we hypothesize that the time required to validate a new build will decrease. This will allow developers to merge and deploy code with greater speed and confidence, reducing the burden on manual QA and catching critical bugs earlier in the development cycle.

## Must have scope

- Automated test coverage for all critical, high-impact features currently covered by manual regression.
- Framework must be built to support the React/TypeScript client, specifically interacting with GraphQL and Apollo.
- Integration with a designated test management tool to report test results and status.
- Ability for developers to run tests locally for quick verification.
- Integration into the nightly build on Travis CI, running alongside existing API tests.
- Parallel test execution to minimize total run time.
- Test data setup and teardown must be performed via the API to ensure a clean state and reduce execution time.
- Ability to execute tests for different user roles (e.g., admin, standard user, guest) with minimal overhead - storing credentials etc.

## Stakeholders

- Product: Ensures the automated tests align with product requirements and business priorities.
- Front-end Developers: Will be the primary users of the framework for local testing and will contribute new test cases.
- QA/Manual Testers: Will define the test cases to be automated and rely on the results for regression validation.
- DevOps Engineer: Will be responsible for integrating the test suite into the CI/CD pipeline on Travis CI.
- 

## Design
The automation framework will be built using the Playwright framework from Microsoft, chosen for its robust support for modern web applications and parallel execution. API-driven data setup will be implemented by using a custom library or directly making GraphQL mutations/queries before each test to create the necessary state. The framework will also include a reporter configured to provide detailed reports on key criteria such as test duration and the number of failed tests. To support different user roles, the framework will have a mechanism to dynamically log in as the desired user type, likely by using API authentication to retrieve a session token before each test. Furthermore, the framework will leverage Playwright's network interception capabilities to report on service interactions, providing visibility into the performance and responses of GraphQL and REST API calls. Parallel execution will be configured via Playwright's test runner, with tests distributed across multiple workers to run concurrently.
t: QA: Client Automation (UI) (M)

## Description
This Epic enables users to **set up and populate Spaces using AI assistance**.
Through a conversational interface, a user (facilitator, community lead, or new contributor) can get help with:
- Designing the **structure** of their Space (Spaces, Subspaces, themes, goals)
- **Populating** their Space with content (Callouts, descriptions, visuals, example posts)
- Discovering **best practices** from other similar Spaces

The AI acts as a **co-pilot** that helps users create well-structured, engaging, and purpose-driven Spaces — faster and with higher quality.


## Goal
Reduce the barrier to create a high-quality Space, and thereby:
- Increase the **activation rate** of new Spaces (Spaces becoming active with members and content).
- Improve the **quality of content** through AI-supported writing and structure.
- Give users an early sense of **momentum** and **clarity** in their collaboration.

## Hypothesis
If users receive AI assistance when creating and filling their Space, then:
- The % of **active Spaces** will increase.
- The **average time** between “Space created” and “first Callout” will decrease.
- Users will perceive their onboarding and first collaboration as more intuitive and inspiring.

## Must have scope
**MVP functionality:**
- [ ] Chat interface for guiding the user through Space setup
- [ ] AI suggests:
  - [ ] Structural setup (Spaces, Subspaces)
  - [ ] Content (Why, Who, Community Guidelines, First Callouts)
  - [ ] Visuals (banners)
- [ ] With a press on a button the suggested structure is transformed into an actual space

**Nice-to-have / Stretch goals:**
- [ ] AI recognizes context from existing Spaces (“You seem to be creating a Space about climate innovation — would you like to see examples from similar Spaces?”)
- [ ] Multi-language prompt and output support


## Stakeholders
- Product Manager for overall coordination of this Epic
- Denise/Maloe for best practices in generating Spaces
- Jeroen for design
- Dev team for development

## Description
Introduce managed file storage with a familiar folder-based structure (similar to OneDrive/Google Drive). Users can create folders, upload files, organize them, and control access—within existing spaces or communities. Files and folders can include hyperlinks to relevant entities (e.g., Space, Subspace).

## Goal
Make it easy and secure to store, find, and share files inside the platform, reducing reliance on external drives and scattered links.

## Hypothesis
If users can manage files with a simple folder structure and basic controls inside the platform, then:
- content will be easier to find (↓ time to find a file),
- duplication/confusion will drop (↓ duplicate uploads),
- adoption and engagement will increase (↑ active users interacting with files).

## Must have scope
- **Folder structure:** create, rename, delete folders; breadcrumbs; path shown.
- **File operations:** upload, download, rename, move, delete; drag-and-drop.
- **Permissions:** inherit from Space/Group by default; optional folder-level overrides (view/upload/manage).
- **Search & filters:** search by name; filter by type (doc, image, pdf), size, last modified.
- **Quotas & limits:** enforce max file size and total storage per Space (configurable).

## Optional scope
- **Previews:** quick preview for common types (images, PDF, text/markdown).
- **Links:** copy internal link; add hyperlinks from files/folders to entities (e.g., Space, Subspace, Callout); respect permissions.
- **Compliance & safety basics:** virus scan on upload; file type allowlist; required metadata (owner, created/modified).

TBD

## Description  
We want to introduce **roles** for template packs— such as **Host**, **Content Provider**, and **Expert** — to improve how templates are managed and used across the platform.  

- **Hosts** will be responsible for making template packs available and maintaining them on the platform.  
- **Content Providers** (e.g. organizations or networks) can contribute templates without needing to take responsibility for publishing or updating them.  
- **Experts** can be linked to a template pack to help users understand or apply the templates, which could create a business case for these experts (e.g. visibility, consulting leads, or monetization).  

This setup allows Alkemio to use a wider range of templates while reducing the operational overhead for template providers, and it helps users connect with relevant experts.  

---

## Goal  
Enable scalable use and curation of high-quality template packs without requiring every template provider to manage their own pack.  
Additionally, improve engagement and learning by connecting users to experts related to the templates.  

This supports Alkemio’s broader initiative to grow its **knowledge base** and **network effect**, while enabling more organizations and individuals to contribute value without friction.  

---

## Hypothesis  
If we allow Alkemio (and possibly others) to host template packs on behalf of providers and link experts to these packs:  
- We can significantly increase the number of high-quality templates available on the platform.  
- Users will be more likely to engage with templates that are supported or explained by experts.  
- The “expert linking” feature will strengthen the ecosystem by connecting users to people, not just content.  

---

## Must have scope  
- Ability to assign multiple roles to a template pack (Host, Content Provider, Expert).  
- Display assigned roles visibly in the UI.  
- Alkemio (as an entity) can be assigned as a Host for specific packs.  
- Experts can be linked to one or more template packs and discoverable by users.  
- Roles and permissions clearly defined and manageable via template pack settings.  
- Content provider is visible on the cards, not the host
- Search on any of the roles yields all packs of those orgs
---

## Description
This Epic delivers “next level” user-to-user (U2U) messaging in Alkemio by making messaging available directly in the contexts where collaboration happens—especially inside whiteboards. It expands U2U from a standalone chat experience into:
- **Whiteboard-native messaging** (message while you work, without losing context)
- **Whiteboard rooms** (temporary, session-based chat with the people currently collaborating in a whiteboard)
- **Scheduled messages** (send later / reminders / timed follow-ups)

**Primary persona(s)**
- **Member / Collaborator:** wants to quickly coordinate, ask questions, and make decisions while working in a whiteboard.
- **Facilitator / Whiteboard owner:** wants lightweight ways to align people in-session and follow up after.
- **Power users (frequent whiteboard & messaging users):** want faster navigation, fewer context switches, and better continuity from “working together” to “keeping in touch.”

**Job to be done**
“When I’m collaborating in a whiteboard, I want to message the right people immediately (in-context and sometimes temporarily as a group), and schedule follow-ups, so coordination stays effortless and work keeps moving.”

## Goal
Increase collaboration efficiency and continuity by reducing context switching between whiteboards and messaging, improving response rates and follow-through on actions created during collaborative work. This supports the broader initiative of making Alkemio a more “all-in-one” collaboration space where synchronous and asynchronous teamwork connect seamlessly.

## Hypothesis
If we make U2U messaging available directly from whiteboards, add temporary whiteboard rooms for in-session coordination, and enable scheduled messages for follow-up, then:
- More users will communicate during collaboration moments (higher messaging activation from whiteboards)
- Coordination will become faster (shorter time-to-first-response and fewer dropped threads)
- Users will return more frequently (improved retention for users who use whiteboards)

**Success measures**
- % of whiteboard sessions that generate at least 1 message (whiteboard → messaging conversion)
- Time-to-first-message from opening a whiteboard
- Time-to-first-response in whiteboard-initiated threads
- 7-day and 28-day retention uplift for users who use whiteboard messaging vs. those who don’t
- Scheduled message usage (creation rate + send completion rate)

**Leading indicators**
- Clicks on “Message” entry points inside whiteboards
- Room creation / join rate during active whiteboard sessions
- Messages per active whiteboard session
- Repeat use: users who use whiteboard messaging 2+ times within 14 days
- Qualitative: fewer reported “had to switch tools” moments in interviews/support tickets

## Must have scope
- **U2U access from whiteboards**
  - Entry point(s) from whiteboard UI (e.g., toolbar, participant list, contextual user avatar)
  - Start 1:1 chat with a participant without leaving the whiteboard (overlay/drawer)
  - Preserve context (link to whiteboard, optional selection reference)

- **Whiteboard rooms (temporary chat)**
  - Create/join a room tied to a whiteboard session
  - Auto-suggest participants currently active in the whiteboard
  - Clear “temporary” behavior definition (e.g., archived after X days or after session ends; searchable rules)
  - Basic moderation/ownership rules (who can create, who can invite, who can remove)

- **Scheduled messages**
  - Schedule send-time in U2U (and optionally room chat)
  - Edit/cancel scheduled message before send
  - Handle timezone and delivery confirmation states (scheduled / sent / failed)

- **Core UX + reliability**
  - Notifications for messages initiated from whiteboards
  - Permissions aligned with whiteboard access (only message people you can collaborate with / or per existing U2U rules)
  - Basic analytics instrumentation for success metrics above

## Stakeholders
- **Product:** PM (owner), Design, Research
- **Engineering:** Tech lead, FE (whiteboard + messaging surfaces), BE (messaging + scheduling), QA
- **Customer Success / Support:** need messaging changes, expected customer questions, release comms + known limitations
- **Community / Ops (if applicable):** guidance on collaboration etiquette / moderation for rooms
- **Growth / Data:** tracking plan, dashboards, experiment design (if A/B testing)
- **Security / Privacy (if applicable):** review of permissions, data retention for rooms, scheduled message delivery guarantees

# Feature Specification: Space Todo Lists

**Feature Branch**:  20-space-todo-lists
**Created**: 2025-12-16
**Status**: Draft
**Input**: User description: 'I want to build a feature where you can have to do lists in your space and subspace. A user can then see on his dashboard (alkem.io/home) which actions are open for him/her. This list retreives all to do''s from all the (sub)spaces the person is member from. We''ll have a separate block with to do''s, which will appear on space home tab by default, below the calendar. Each to do action has: an owner (someone can be tagged (e.g. @username), a title, a descritpion, and a status (open/closed)), and a due date. UI can be very simple at first. When a to do item has a due date, it will be added to the calendar of the individual (I also want a calendar on the dashboard that collects all calendar events from someones spaces/subspaces).'

## User Scenarios & Testing *(mandatory)*

### User Story 1 - View Personal Dashboard Todos (Priority: P1)

As a User, I want to see a list of all my assigned todos from all spaces I am a member of on my personal dashboard, so that I know what I need to work on across the platform.

**Why this priority**: This is the core value proposition for the individual user to manage their work.

**Independent Test**: Can be tested by creating todos in different spaces assigned to a user and verifying they appear on the user's dashboard.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** I am logged in and on  lkem.io/home, **When** I view the dashboard, **Then** I see a "My Todos" section.
2. **Given** I have assigned todos in Space A and Space B, **When** I view the "My Todos" section, **Then** I see todos from both spaces listed.
3. **Given** I have no assigned todos, **When** I view the section, **Then** I see an empty state message indicating no pending tasks.

---

### User Story 2 - Manage Space Todos (Priority: P1)

As a Space Member, I want to view, create, and update todos within a space, so that we can track tasks specific to that space.

**Why this priority**: Essential for creating the data that feeds into the dashboard and for space-level collaboration.

**Independent Test**: Can be tested within a single space by creating and modifying todos.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** I am on a Space Home tab, **When** I scroll below the calendar, **Then** I see the "Space Todos" block.
2. **Given** I am on the Space Todos block, **When** I click "Add Todo", **Then** I can enter a title, description, assignee (selecting a member), and due date.
3. **Given** a todo exists, **When** I change its status to "Closed", **Then** it is visually marked as closed/completed.
4. **Given** a todo exists, **When** I edit the assignee, **Then** the new assignee is saved.

---

### User Story 3 - Unified Personal Calendar (Priority: P2)

As a User, I want to see my todos with due dates and all space events on my personal dashboard calendar, so that I have a unified view of my schedule.

**Why this priority**: Enhances the dashboard utility by combining tasks and events.

**Independent Test**: Can be tested by verifying the personal calendar view against created space events and dated todos.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** I have a todo with a due date, **When** I view my personal dashboard calendar, **Then** I see the todo displayed as an item on that date.
2. **Given** I am a member of spaces with calendar events, **When** I view my personal dashboard calendar, **Then** I see those events displayed.
3. **Given** I am not a member of a space, **When** I view my personal dashboard calendar, **Then** I do not see events from that space.

### Edge Cases

- What happens when a user is removed from a space? Their assigned todos from that space should likely disappear from their dashboard or be reassigned (Assumed: they disappear from personal view but remain in space).
- How does the system handle todos with deleted assignees?
- What happens if a due date is set in the past?
- How many todos can be displayed on the dashboard before pagination or "load more" is needed?

## Dependencies and Assumptions

- **Assumption**: When a user is removed from a space, their assigned todos remain in the space but are no longer visible on their personal dashboard.
- **Assumption**: The "Calendar" mentioned refers to the existing calendar functionality in spaces.
- **Dependency**: This feature depends on the existing Space and User membership models.

## Success Criteria

- **SC-001**: Users can view their aggregated todos on the dashboard within 2 seconds of loading.
- **SC-002**: Space members can create a new todo in under 30 seconds.
- **SC-003**: 100% of assigned todos with due dates appear on the personal calendar.
- **SC-004**: Users report a unified view of their tasks and events reduces the need to navigate to individual spaces.

## Requirements *(mandatory)*

### Functional Requirements

- **FR-001**: System MUST allow creating a Todo item within a Space or Subspace context.
- **FR-002**: A Todo item MUST have the following fields: Title, Description, Status (Open/Closed), Assignee (User reference), and Due Date (optional).
- **FR-003**: System MUST display a list of Todos associated with the *current* Space (excluding subspaces) on the Space Home tab, positioned below the calendar.
- **FR-004**: System MUST display a list of Todos assigned to the current user on the User's Personal Dashboard ( lkem.io/home).
- **FR-005**: The Personal Dashboard Todo list MUST aggregate assigned todos from all spaces and subspaces the user is a member of.
- **FR-006**: System MUST allow authorized users (e.g., creator, assignee, space admin) to update the status of a Todo (Open/Closed).
- **FR-007**: System MUST allow assigning a Todo to a specific member of the space.
- **FR-008**: System MUST display Todos that have a Due Date on the User's Personal Dashboard Calendar.
- **FR-009**: System MUST aggregate all calendar events from all spaces/subspaces the user is a member of and display them on the User's Personal Dashboard Calendar.
- **FR-010**: System MUST send a notification to the assignee when a Todo is assigned to them.
- **FR-011**: System MUST send a notification to the assignee when the status of their assigned Todo changes.
- **FR-012**: System MUST allow the Creator, Assignee, and Space Admins to edit the details (Title, Description, Due Date) of a Todo item.
- **FR-013**: System MUST display a maximum of 10 Todo items initially in the Space Home block and Personal Dashboard, with a mechanism to load more (e.g., pagination or "Show More").
- **FR-014**: System MUST display Todo items sorted by Created Date in descending order (newest first) by default.

### Key Entities *(include if feature involves data)*

- **TodoItem**: Represents a task unit.
    - id: Unique identifier
    - spaceId: Reference to the containing Space/Subspace
    - 	itle: Short text summary
    - description: Detailed text
    - status: Enum (OPEN, CLOSED)
    -  ssigneeId: Reference to User (nullable)
    - dueDate: Timestamp (nullable)
    - createdAt: Timestamp
    - updatedAt: Timestamp

## Clarifications

### Session 2025-12-16

- Q: Should users be notified when assigned a todo or when its status changes?  A: Notify assignee on assignment and status change.
- Q: Who is allowed to edit the details (title, description, due date) of a todo item?  A: Creator, Assignee, and Space Admins.
- Q: How many todos should be displayed initially on the dashboard and space home?  A: 10 items.
- Q: Should the Space Home todo list include items from subspaces?  A: Current space only.
- Q: What is the default sort order for the todo list?  A: Created Date (Descending).

# Epic: Alkemio Native Mobile App

## Description
Epic to bring Alkemio to the app stores as a native mobile app. Starting point: our current mobile-responsive website is already a solid experience, so instead of building native from scratch we explore wrapping it (Capacitor, PWA-to-native, Trusted Web Activity, or similar) to get a real app quickly.

Job story: when a Space admin or member wants to check updates or contribute while away from their laptop, they want an app on their phone instead of opening a browser, so Alkemio feels as accessible as the other tools they use daily.

Messaging gets disproportionate weight in this Epic compared to the website. Similar to LinkedIn's model: one switch or toggle to flip between the main platform view and messages, feeling almost like two apps but tightly integrated. Our current mobile web already has most of the pieces for this; the app should surface and polish that switch experience rather than build it from scratch.

Secondary persona: partners who expect an app-store presence as a baseline sign of a "real" platform, separate from the actual UX gain.

## Goal
Increase engagement and reach by lowering the barrier to open Alkemio: home screen icon, push notifications, faster re-entry. Also strengthens credibility with public sector partners who associate app-store presence with maturity; ties into the "tech for good" credibility work.

## Hypothesis
Wrapping the existing mobile web experience is fast enough to validate demand before investing in a fully native build. If we get into both stores and see meaningful installs plus repeat opens (vs. one-time curiosity), that tells us it's worth investing further.

Messaging and push are the sharpest leading indicators here, not side notes: if the messaging switch experience drives real usage and push opt-in/click-through is healthy, that's a strong signal the app earns a spot on someone's home screen rather than being a novelty. If those numbers are flat, the wrapper approach probably isn't enough on its own.

## Must have scope

- [ ] Working native wrapper of current mobile web app, functional login/session
- [ ] Messaging switch experience: a single, prominent control to flip between platform and messages, LinkedIn-style, built on what already exists in mobile web
- [ ] Push notifications in v1
- [ ] App icon, splash screen, basic branding
- [ ] Apple Developer Program enrollment and app submitted to App Store
- [ ] Google Play Console account and app submitted to Play Store
- [ ] Graceful handling of anything that doesn't work well in a wrapped context (e.g. file uploads, external auth redirects)

Open item for planning: push notifications in v1 means an early decision on the underlying service (native push via APNs/FCM directly, or something like OneSignal/Firebase Cloud Messaging wrapping both). 

## Important: sign-off on direction and store enrollment (Apple requires organisation legal details and a D-U-N-S number; this takes time, worth starting now)

## Items noted by Bobby
The SSO blocker.
The self-deletion feature. 
App notifications - it's the feature that could justify why we submit our website in the stores.
Fix/provide all visual assets - big amount of assets included in the builds but also screenshots for the Store pages.
Full mobile testing - discover what flows and features need fixing e.g.:
Revisit the back navigation on mobile - device specific, no breadcrumbs, no exit from auth pages etc.
Missing interactions on hover - e.g. add reaction to chat message.
t: Alkemio "native" mobile app

## Description

Replace the data access layer from TypeORM (custom fork) to Drizzle ORM + postgres.js across the server codebase. This eliminates the dependency on a custom TypeORM fork, provides full type-safe queries, lighter runtime overhead, and native ESM compatibility — aligning with the broader server stack modernization effort.

Part of the **Server Stack Modernization** milestone alongside:
- [alkemio#1536](https://github.com/alkem-io/alkemio/issues/1536) — Phase 1 & 2: NestJS 11, Apollo 5, Node 24
- [alkemio#1790](https://github.com/alkem-io/alkemio/issues/1790) — Phase 3: NestJS 12 + ESM Migration

### The primary job to be done is:
- As a backend engineer, I want to replace TypeORM with Drizzle ORM so that we remove the custom fork dependency, gain full type-safe queries, and prepare the data layer for ESM migration.

### Secondary:
- As a product team, we want to ensure database operations remain reliable and performant during and after the migration.

## Current Progress

A draft PR is already open: **[server#5846](https://github.com/alkem-io/server/pull/5846)** — "Migrate data access layer from TypeORM to Drizzle ORM"

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Files changed | 906 |
| Lines | +74.6k / -14.9k |
| Tables migrated | 75 |
| Modules affected | 97 |
| Tests passing | 495/495 |

### What changes

| Area | Before (TypeORM) | After (Drizzle) |
|---|---|---|
| ORM | TypeORM 0.3 (custom fork) + pg | Drizzle ORM + postgres.js |
| DI pattern | `@InjectRepository()` / `@InjectEntityManager()` | `@Inject(DRIZZLE)` (Symbol token) |
| Queries | Repository methods + QueryBuilder | Drizzle relational (`db.query.*`) + SQL-like API |
| Schema | `@Entity()` decorators | `pgTable()` functional definitions |
| Relations | `@OneToOne()` / `@ManyToOne()` decorators | `relations()` in separate `*.relations.ts` files |
| Cascades | ORM-level `cascade: true` (112 relations) | Explicit service-layer insert/update/delete |
| Eager loading | `eager: true` (25 relations) | Explicit `with:` clauses |
| Migrations | TypeORM CLI | Drizzle Kit (`drizzle-kit generate` / `drizzle-kit migrate`) |
| Test mocks | `repositoryMockFactory` / `MockEntityManagerProvider` | `mockDrizzleProvider` (Proxy-based) |

## Relationship to Other Epics

- **Removes the TypeORM custom fork** — this was flagged as a risk in Phase 1 & 2 (alkemio#1536) since the fork needed rebasing for NestJS 11
- **Enables ESM migration** — Drizzle has native ESM support; TypeORM had circular dependency issues in ESM requiring `Relation` wrapper types
- **Should ideally land before or alongside Phase 1** to avoid rebasing the Drizzle migration on top of NestJS 11 changes (or vice versa)

## Goal

This Epic supports the initiative to maintain a modern and well-supported backend stack, reduce tech debt, and ensure compatibility with new libraries and tools. Replacing the custom TypeORM fork removes a significant maintenance burden and unblocks the ESM migration path.

## Hypothesis

If we migrate from TypeORM to Drizzle ORM, then our data access layer will be more type-safe, performant, and maintainable — while eliminating the risk of maintaining a custom ORM fork.

Success metrics:
- All services build and deploy successfully post-migration
- Test suites pass with no regressions
- Schema parity confirmed via `drizzle-kit generate` (zero-diff migration)
- No production issues within two weeks post-release
- Custom TypeORM fork fully removed from dependencies

## Must Have Scope

- Complete migration of all 75 tables from TypeORM entities to Drizzle schema definitions
- Replace all repository/entity manager injections with Drizzle DI
- Replace all QueryBuilder usages with Drizzle query APIs
- Migrate all cascading operations to explicit service-layer logic
- Remove TypeORM packages, config, migration infrastructure, and test utilities
- Full E2E testing against the production schema
- Documentation of migration patterns in `specs/034-drizzle-migration/`

## Risk Areas

| Area | Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| 906 files changed | Large blast radius | Comprehensive test suite (495 tests), schema parity check |
| Cascade removal | Implicit cascades replaced with explicit logic | Audit all 112 cascade relations |
| Merge conflicts | Large PR may conflict with ongoing work | Coordinate merge timing with other epics |
| Drizzle pre-1.0 | v1.0 still in beta | 0.x API has been stable; 4-5M weekly npm downloads |
| Performance | Different query patterns | Drizzle has near-zero runtime overhead; benchmark in specs |

## Stakeholders

- Engineering – core backend team (responsible for implementation)
- DevOps – ensure build & deployment remains stable
- Product – for awareness of possible temporary slowdowns in feature delivery
- QA – to validate stability and regression coverage

## Design
Figma file: N/A – This Epic is technical and does not include UI work.
Full specification available in `specs/034-drizzle-migration/` in the server repo.
t: ORM layer switch to Drizzle

## Summary

Evaluate and select a tool (or combination of tools) for automated **license compliance**, **vulnerability scanning**, and **security analysis** across Alkemio repositories. The solution should ideally be **European, self-hosted, and OSS-licensed**.

## Context

We currently rely on GitHub Dependabot for security updates, but lack a comprehensive solution for:
- License compliance checking across all dependencies
- SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation
- Automated vulnerability scanning beyond npm audit
- Policy enforcement (e.g. blocklisting certain licenses)

## Tools to Evaluate

### 1. OSS Review Toolkit (ORT)
- **License:** Apache 2.0 (Linux Foundation / ACT project)
- **Origin:** European contributors, Eclipse Apoapsis server variant
- **Deployment:** Fully self-hosted (CLI + ORT Server via Eclipse Apoapsis)
- **Capabilities:** Dependency analysis (20+ package managers), license scanning, vulnerability advisory, policy engine, SBOM generation (CycloneDX, SPDX)
- **Links:** [ORT](https://oss-review-toolkit.org/ort/) · [GitHub](https://github.com/oss-review-toolkit/ort) · [ORT Server](https://github.com/eclipse-apoapsis/ort-server)

### 2. Trivy (Aqua Security)
- **License:** Apache 2.0
- **Origin:** Israel (Aqua Security)
- **Deployment:** Self-hosted, lightweight CLI
- **Capabilities:** Vulnerability scanning (OS packages, language deps, container images), license scanning, secret detection, IaC misconfiguration, SBOM generation
- **Links:** [trivy.dev](https://trivy.dev/) · [GitHub](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy)

### 3. FOSSology
- **License:** GPL 2.0 (Linux Foundation)
- **Origin:** Originally HP, now LF community project
- **Deployment:** Self-hosted (Docker), web UI + REST API
- **Capabilities:** Deep license scanning, copyright detection, export control, SPDX generation, deduplication for rescans
- **Links:** [fossology.org](https://www.fossology.org/) · [GitHub](https://github.com/fossology/fossology)

### 4. Eclipse SW360
- **License:** EPL 2.0 (Eclipse Foundation)
- **Origin:** European (Eclipse Foundation, Siemens, Bosch contributors)
- **Deployment:** Self-hosted, web application
- **Capabilities:** Component catalog, license tracking, SBOM import (SPDX), integrates with FOSSology for license clearing
- **Links:** [eclipse.dev/sw360](https://eclipse.dev/sw360/) · [GitHub](https://github.com/eclipse-sw360/sw360)

### 5. Aikido Security
- **License:** Commercial (some OSS components)
- **Origin:** Belgian (European)
- **Deployment:** SaaS + self-hosted scanner option
- **Capabilities:** SCA with reachability analysis, SAST, license risk, container scanning, cloud posture
- **Links:** [aikido.dev](https://www.aikido.dev/) · [GitHub](https://github.com/AikidoSec)

## Evaluation Criteria

| Criterion | Weight | Notes |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| License compliance scanning | High | Must detect and report OSS licenses in all transitive deps |
| Vulnerability scanning | High | CVE database coverage, advisory sources |
| SBOM generation | High | CycloneDX and/or SPDX support |
| Self-hosted / on-prem | High | No mandatory SaaS dependency |
| OSS license | High | Apache 2.0, EPL, or similar permissive license preferred |
| European origin / GDPR | Medium | Preference for EU-based projects |
| CI/CD integration | Medium | GitHub Actions, CLI-based, easy to automate |
| Policy engine | Medium | Ability to define allowed/blocked licenses, severity thresholds |
| Multi-ecosystem support | Medium | npm, Docker, Python, etc. |
| Ease of setup & maintenance | Medium | Docker-based, documentation quality |
| Active community & maintenance | Low | Release cadence, contributor activity |

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Each tool has been evaluated hands-on (at least a PoC scan against one Alkemio repo)
- [ ] Comparison matrix filled in with scores per criterion
- [ ] Recommendation documented with rationale
- [ ] Cost analysis (infra for self-hosting vs commercial licensing if applicable)
- [ ] Decision recorded
t: Evaluate OSS license, vulnerability & security scanning tools

## Phases Overview

### Phase 1 — Apollo 5 + NestJS 11 (alkemio#1536)
Upgrade the core framework and GraphQL stack. Can be done together since `@nestjs/apollo@13.x` bridges both.

### Phase 2 — Node 24 (alkemio#1536)
Upgrade the runtime to Node.js 24 LTS after Phase 1 stabilizes.

### Phase 3 — NestJS 12 + ESM Migration (this epic, deferred to ~Q3 2026)
Upgrade to NestJS 12 and migrate from CommonJS to ESM once NestJS 12 ships native support.

## Description
Upgrade to NestJS 12 and migrate the server codebase and related services from CommonJS to ESM modules. **This should be deferred until NestJS 12 ships native ESM support (~Q3 2026).** NestJS 12 is not yet released as of March 2026.

### The primary job to be done is:
- As a backend engineer, I want to upgrade to NestJS 12 and use ESM so that we can adopt the latest packages (many of which are ESM-only) and align with the modern Node.js ecosystem.

## Scope

**NestJS 12 upgrade:**
- Upgrade `@nestjs/*` from 11.x → 12.x
- Adopt native ESM support as the default module system
- Migrate from Jest to Vitest + SWC (new default for ESM projects in NestJS 12)
- Evaluate Standard Schema support in route decorators (Zod, Valibot, ArkType)

**ESM migration:**
- Migrate tsconfig `module` from `commonjs` to ESM output
- Add `"type": "module"` to package.json
- Update `moduleResolution` to `node16` or `nodenext`
- Use full relative file paths for imports (e.g., `./index.js`)
- Use the `node:` protocol for Node.js built-in imports
- Replace `graphql-upload@13` with ESM-compatible alternative (`graphql-upload-ts` or `graphql-upload@17`)
- Wrap TypeORM entity relations with `Relation` type to avoid circular dependency issues
- Audit and update all ESM-only / CJS-only dependencies
- Update build scripts and Dockerfile if needed

## Key Findings

- NestJS 12 (~Q3 2026) will make ESM the default module system
- NestJS 12 will include: native ESM, Vitest + SWC as default test runner, Standard Schema support
- Node 24's `require(esm)` improves interop, easing the transition
- `graphql-upload` v14+ is ESM-only — current v13 is CJS
- `graphql-upload-ts` provides dual CJS+ESM as a bridge option
- TypeORM circular dependencies need `Relation` wrapper in ESM
- Some packages (chalk, node-fetch, ora, execa) have gone ESM-only in recent major versions

## Current State (server repo)

| Component | Current | Target |
|---|---|---|
| NestJS | 11.x (after Phase 1) | 12.x |
| Module system | CommonJS | ESM |
| tsconfig module | commonjs | node16/nodenext |
| Test runner | Jest | Vitest + SWC |
| graphql-upload | 13.0.0 (CJS) | graphql-upload-ts or v17 (ESM) |
| TypeORM | custom fork | Relation wrappers needed |

## Risk Areas

| Area | Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| NestJS 12 maturity | May have early bugs | Wait for patch releases before adopting |
| `graphql-upload` | v14+ ESM-only | Use `graphql-upload-ts` as bridge or upgrade to v17 |
| TypeORM circular deps | Break in ESM | Use `Relation` wrapper type for all entity relations |
| ESM-only packages | May force premature migration | Pin CJS versions until ready |
| Import paths | All relative imports need `.js` extension | Automated codemod or lint rule |
| Jest → Vitest | Test migration effort | Can be done incrementally |

## Dependencies
- Phase 1 (Apollo 5 + NestJS 11) — alkemio#1536
- Phase 2 (Node 24) — alkemio#1536
- NestJS 12 stable release

## Success Metrics
- All services build and deploy successfully with NestJS 12 + ESM
- Test suites pass with no regressions
- No production issues within two weeks post-release
- Able to use latest versions of previously-blocked ESM-only packages

## Stakeholders
- Engineering – core backend team (responsible for implementation)
- DevOps – ensure build & deployment remains stable
- Product – for awareness of possible temporary slowdowns in feature delivery
t: Phase 3: NestJS 12 + ESM Migration

## Outcome

Make `client-web` a first-class Matrix client for messaging data by integrating `matrix-js-sdk` and connecting the browser directly to Synapse. Keep Alkemio as the authorization and conversation control plane.

This is a deliberate split, not removal of `server` or `matrix-adapter`:

```text
DATA PLANE
client-web ── Matrix SSO, sync, history, unread, receipts, migrated messages ──> Synapse

CONTROL PLANE
client-web ── GraphQL ──> server ──> matrix-adapter ──> Synapse
                         create room/conversation; map room; add/remove/leave;
                         governed metadata; lifecycle; reconciliation and repair

BACKEND EVENT PLANE
Synapse ──> matrix-adapter ──> server ──> notifications/audit/business events

RETAINED MEDIA SEAM (initial cutover; #1946)
client-web ── upload/attachment fields ──> server ──> matrix-adapter ──> Synapse
                                                └──── file-service byte store
```

After cutover, Synapse sync is the browser's single source for Matrix room events. Alkemio subscriptions remain for control-plane and non-Matrix domain events; the same Matrix event must not also reach the migrated browser through GraphQL.

## Authentication seam

The normal user experience is transparent: a user already signed in to Alkemio should not see another credential prompt. Technically, the Alkemio OIDC BFF cookie is **not** passed to Synapse. The browser starts Matrix SSO with Synapse; Synapse uses the existing Hydra/Kratos identity chain, receives the established SSO session, and returns a one-time Matrix login result that `matrix-js-sdk` exchanges for a distinct Matrix device/session.

Token persistence, multi-tab sync ownership, logout, user switching, provisioning, refresh/recovery, redirect validation, and credential redaction are explicit security decisions in the architecture ticket.

## In scope

- `matrix-js-sdk` client/session lifecycle in `client-web`.
- Direct timelines, pagination/history, live sync, unread/highlight counts, read receipts, typing/presence where approved, and room membership projection.
- Direct send, reply, edit, redact, react, and other explicitly migrated non-media message operations.
- Retention of #1946's as-built attachment seam in the first cutover: web upload/canonicalization, server authorization/re-homing/read resolution, and stateless adapter byte/event bridging. Matrix sync owns the media room event; retained GraphQL enrichment must not duplicate it.
- Alkemio-governed room creation, room mapping, add/remove/leave membership, authorization, lifecycle, metadata, reconciliation, and repair.
- Synapse/module/power-level enforcement that prevents normal clients bypassing governed create/invite/kick operations.
- Continued adapter/server processing for notifications, audit/business events, reconciliation, and Element interoperability.
- Cohort rollout, observable comparison, rollback, consumer inventory, and eventual retirement of only the replaced proxy surfaces.

## Delivery slices

### Architecture and senior Matrix/backend ownership

- [ ] alkem-io/alkemio#2075 — Matrix/OIDC browser session and security contract (senior Matrix/OIDC owner; prerequisite)
- [ ] alkem-io/infrastructure-operations#2590 — browser-safe Synapse SSO/client surface and environment parity
- [ ] alkem-io/matrix-adapter#69 — governed control-plane enforcement, membership, reconciliation, and event bridge (senior adapter/backend owner)

### Frontend ownership

- [ ] alkem-io/client-web#10157 — SDK foundation and Matrix session lifecycle
- [ ] alkem-io/client-web#10158 — direct sync/read path: timeline, history, unread, receipts, live events
- [ ] alkem-io/client-web#10159 — direct message operations and Element interoperability

### Backend continuity and retirement

- [ ] alkem-io/server#6378 — retain control contracts; inventory/deprecate only replaced message proxy contracts
- [ ] alkem-io/server#6379 — notifications and platform-event continuity for direct Matrix activity

### Acceptance and rollout

- [ ] alkem-io/test-suites#609 — cross-client security, performance, rollout, fallback, and retirement gates

### Post-epic follow-up

- alkem-io/alkemio#2076 — after #1801 is delivered and direct Matrix media is proven, inventory and retire only the unused #1946 web proxy arm. This is deliberately related rather than a sub-issue, so it does not create a circular epic completion dependency.

## Existing outcome tickets

These remain relevant outcomes enabled by the architecture, but they are not the implementation decomposition:

- [ ] #2015 — Chat created but missing room
- [ ] alkem-io/client-web#9501 — PWA notification for conversation messages

## Ordered gates

1. Accept and prove the Matrix/OIDC/security contract.
2. Close governance and membership-revocation gaps; direct clients cannot bypass Alkemio authorization.
3. Expose and observe the supported Synapse browser surface in non-production environments.
4. Land the frontend SDK lifecycle behind a default-off cohort flag.
5. Shadow-sync and compare state without rendering it.
6. Cut over conversation reads/subscriptions for a controlled cohort.
7. Cut over supported writes and prove backend notification/event continuity.
8. Decide explicitly whether posts/comments/other Matrix-backed rooms migrate or remain on the established path.
9. Expand cohorts only while SSO, authorization, duplication, latency, notification, and rollback gates remain green.
10. After 14 days of full adoption with zero migrated-web proxy traffic, begin separately reviewed proxy retirement. Retain all control-plane and backend-event responsibilities.

Media-specific proxy retirement follows separately in #2076 after this epic's
direct Matrix delivery and its own direct-media/security prerequisites are met.

## Dependencies and related work

- Web-client OIDC foundation alkem-io/server#5612 is complete; this epic must not describe it as future work.
- Membership access revocation alkem-io/server#6329 is a rollout blocker or must be absorbed and demonstrably closed by matrix-adapter#69.
- #1946 is implemented but unmerged behind `communications.message_attachments.enabled`, default off. Its as-built server/adapter attachment seam is retained initially rather than silently reimplemented in `matrix-js-sdk`.
- #1996 is a hard prerequisite for enabling #1946's production media storage cutover (before PV → emptyDir); it does not block the non-media Matrix-native slices of this epic.
- Parent product outcome: #1785. Broader architecture context: #1693.

## Success / exit criteria

- Healthy signed-in users enter Matrix messaging without another interactive prompt.
- All timeline events and explicitly migrated non-media writes go browser-to-Synapse; governed operations and the explicitly retained #1946 attachment seam still go through Alkemio.
- Web ↔ Element tests show no missing or duplicate events across 100 consecutive operations per supported type.
- Online recipient visibility is at most 2 seconds p95 under the agreed acceptance load.
- Complete accessible pre-cutover history remains available without message-copy migration.

## Description
Critical improvements to the virtual-contributor RAG pipeline addressing chunk sizing, retrieval quality, and hierarchy-aware ingestion. Analysis compared the current Python port against the original TypeScript/Python repositories and current RAG research (2024-2026 benchmarks).

**Key findings:**
- Space chunk_size (9,000 chars / ~2,250 tokens) is 2-5x larger than every benchmark's optimal range (400-1,024 tokens)
- The port removed compensating mechanisms from the originals (LLM-based source scoring, `[source:N]` formatting) while increasing retrieval volume (n_results 4→10)
- Summaries and raw chunks compete in the same flat ChromaDB collection with no metadata filtering — and no retrieval code path ever uses summaries intentionally (true in originals too)
- The 3-level space hierarchy (Space → Subspace → Callout → Contribution) is completely flattened during ingestion — no parent-child metadata preserved
- No distance/score threshold filtering on retrieval; no context window budgeting before LLM calls

## Key Research References
- [Anthropic: Contextual Retrieval (2024)](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval) — 49% retrieval failure reduction with context enrichment + BM25
- [arXiv:2603.06976](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.06976) — "performance degrades monotonically with increasing token span"
- [GDELT Embedding Length Study](https://blog.gdeltproject.org/embedding-models-the-impact-of-textual-length-on-embedding-similarity-part-2/) — 21% similarity drop for long vs short passages
- [LlamaIndex Chunk Size Evaluation](https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/evaluating-the-ideal-chunk-size-for-a-rag-system-using-llamaindex-6207e5d3fec5) — 512-1024 tokens optimal
- [Chroma Context Rot (2025)](https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-rot) — LLM degradation at 2,500-5,000 words of context
- [RAPTOR (UC Berkeley 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.18059) — hierarchical summary tree retrieval
- [HyDE (Gao et al., 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10496) — hypothetical document embeddings for query-document bridging
- [Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511) — self-reflective retrieval-augmented generation
- [Corrective RAG (Yan et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884) — retrieval quality evaluation and correction
- [RankGPT (Sun et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.09542) — LLM-based listwise passage re-ranking
- [RAGAS (Es et al., 2024)](https://docs.ragas.io) — RAG evaluation framework
- [Adaptive RAG (Jeong et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14403) — complexity-based retrieval routing

## Stakeholders
Virtual Contributor / AI team

## Description

The ingest pipeline ACKs RabbitMQ messages only after the entire pipeline completes (crawl → chunk → summarize → embed → upsert → BoK summary). For content-heavy sites, the pipeline can exceed RabbitMQ's `consumer_timeout`, causing infinite redelivery loops.

### Observed Incident (2026-04-07)

A single ingest trigger for the Alkemio Guidance VC resulted in:
- **30 redeliveries** over 15 hours (exactly every 30 minutes — the default `consumer_timeout`)
- **4,299 LLM API calls** (vs ~150 expected for a single pass)
- The pipeline never completed because each 30-minute cycle was insufficient

### Current Workaround
`consumer_timeout` increased to 2 hours. This is a band-aid — a sufficiently large corpus or slower model will hit the same wall.

## Proposed Solution

Decouple message acknowledgment from pipeline completion:

1. Consumer receives message
2. Validates message schema
3. **ACKs immediately** ("I received a valid message, don't redeliver")
4. Runs pipeline asynchronously
5. Publishes result to result queue on completion (success or failure)

### Risk: Lost Messages
With early ACK, if the process crashes mid-pipeline, the message is gone. Mitigation:
- Result queue provides completeness check
- Server can re-trigger if no result arrives within timeout
- Idempotent processing (content-hash dedup) means re-triggers are safe

## Additional Requirement: Outer Timeout

Independent of early ACK, `main.on_message()` (main.py:279-303) needs an outer `asyncio.wait_for()` timeout wrapping the entire `plugin.handle()` call. Individual LLM calls have 120s timeouts, but there's no timeout on the pipeline as a whole.

## Location
- `core/adapters/rabbitmq.py` — message ACK location
- `main.py:279-303` — `on_message` callback
- Full PRD: `specs/008-early-ack-async-processing/prd.md`

## Parent
alkem-io/alkemio#1820
t: Early ACK with async processing — decouple message acknowledgment from pipeline completion

## Problem

Website ingestion is currently triggered via `refreshVirtualContributorBodyOfKnowledge(vcId)`, which:

1. **URLs are hardcoded** in `ai.server.service.ts:132-147` — three static URLs for the GUIDANCE engine only
2. **No URL storage** — website sources aren't stored anywhere (not in DB, not in VC entity)
3. **No ingestion parameters** — can't control page limits, depth, or URL filtering
4. **Only works for GUIDANCE engine** — impossible to create a new website-backed VC
5. **No standalone ingest API** — website ingestion is buried inside a generic "refresh" mutation
6. **Three messages fired blindly** — no coordination, no progress tracking

## Proposed Solution

### New GraphQL Mutation

```graphql
mutation IngestWebsite($input: IngestWebsiteInput!) {
  ingestWebsite(input: $input): IngestWebsiteJobResult!
}

input IngestWebsiteInput {
  """Target VC whose knowledge base receives the ingested content"""
  virtualContributorID: UUID!

  """One or more website sources to crawl"""
  sources: [WebsiteSourceInput!]!

  """FULL: wipe collection first. INCREMENTAL: only add/update changed content."""
  mode: IngestionMode = INCREMENTAL
}

input WebsiteSourceInput {
  """Base URL to start crawling from"""
  url: String!

  """Max pages to crawl from this source (-1 = unlimited)"""
  pageLimit: Int = 20

  """Max link depth from base URL (0 = base page only, -1 = unlimited)"""
  maxDepth: Int = -1

  """Only crawl URLs matching these glob patterns (e.g. ["/docs/*"])"""
  includePatterns: [String!]

  """Skip URLs matching these glob patterns (e.g. ["/admin/*", "*.pdf"])"""
  excludePatterns: [String!]
}

enum IngestionMode {
  FULL
  INCREMENTAL
}

type IngestWebsiteJobResult {
  """Job ID for tracking progress"""
  jobID: UUID!
  status: IngestionJobStatus!
}

enum IngestionJobStatus {
  QUEUED
  CRAWLING
  SUMMARIZING
  EMBEDDING
  STORING
  COMPLETED
  FAILED
}
```

### Job Status Query

```graphql
type Query {
  ingestionJob(jobID: UUID!): IngestionJob
}

type IngestionJob {
  id: UUID!
  status: IngestionJobStatus!
  sources: [IngestionSourceProgress!]!
  startedAt: DateTime
  completedAt: DateTime
  error: String
}

type IngestionSourceProgress {
  url: String!
  pagesCrawled: Int!
  chunksProcessed: Int!
}
```

## Architecture: Domain Boundary

The Alkemio server is a **thin pass-through** for ingestion requests — it validates the VC exists, checks authorization, and publishes the request to RabbitMQ. It does NOT:
- Store website sources, crawl configs, or chunking params in the platform DB
- Own any RAG/AI-specific domain logic

All processing details (chunking, summarization, embedding, distance functions) are owned by the virtual-contributor service.

### Refresh Flow (Option A — VC service remembers sources)

The existing `refreshVirtualContributorBodyOfKnowledge` mutation stays as a convenience shortcut. For WEBSITE-type VCs, the **virtual-contributor service** remembers the last-ingested sources (e.g., in ChromaDB collection metadata or a sidecar store) and re-uses them on refresh. The platform never stores crawl configuration.

This keeps the domain boundary clean: the platform knows "this VC has a knowledge base" but not "this VC crawls these URLs with these patterns."

## Implementation Notes

### Server side (alkemio/server)
- New mutation `ingestWebsite` in the VC resolver
- New input DTOs matching the schema above
- Publish enriched `IngestWebsite` message to RabbitMQ with full source config
- Remove hardcoded URL list from `ai.server.service.ts:132-147`
- Job status tracking: either via RabbitMQ result messages or a lightweight job table

### VC service side (virtual-contributor)
- Extend `IngestWebsite` event schema to accept the new fields (pageLimit, maxDepth, patterns)
- Crawler: respect `maxDepth` and `includePatterns`/`excludePatterns`
- Store source config in collection metadata for refresh support
- Report progress back via result queue for job status updates

### Conventions
- `-1` means unlimited everywhere (pageLimit, maxDepth)
- Per-source chunking params are NOT exposed — managed internally by the VC service config

## Out of Scope
- Authenticated crawling (cookies, API keys)
- Crawl type selection (SITEMAP, SINGLE_PAGE, CRAWL)
- Per-source chunk sizing — managed by VC service env vars
- Storing website sources in the platform DB

## Parent
alkem-io/alkemio#1820
t: First-class website ingestion API — replace hardcoded URLs with configurable GraphQL mutation
