## What & why

The acceptance environment currently carries a large amount of broken/inconsistent data, which undermines testing and demos. We want a **re-runnable process that derives a small, real, internally-consistent acceptance dataset from production** — with a hard, auditable guarantee that **no customer-derived data** lands in acceptance.

Safety posture: **allowlist + reset identities**. Only an explicit, reviewed allowlist of spaces, users, and organisations is carried over (default-deny; everything else excluded), and each retained user's personal identifiers (name, email) are replaced with **deterministic synthetic values** during derivation. A fail-closed verification + leak-scan gate rejects any run that would publish unapproved content or a residual real identifier.

It is explicitly fine for the acceptance dataset to be **much smaller** than production — safety and consistency take precedence over volume.

## Scope highlights

- **Opt-in allowlist** selection: **generic rules** (e.g. "all spaces owned by org X") + **specific** include/exclude, with specific decisions overriding generic; unclassified content excluded and surfaced for review.
- **Per-space permissions list**: for each selected space, an explicit list of which members/roles carry over.
- **Inventory / review** of all production spaces, users, orgs with classification status.
- **Referential consistency** with fail-closed dependency handling (a selected item depending on non-approved content is excluded and reported — never auto-includes).
- **Deterministic identity substitution** (name/email) during derivation; free-form text is a known, accepted residual.
- **Re-runnable & idempotent**, wholesale rebuild that discards broken data; production is **read-only**, never modified.
- **Secrets never copied verbatim**; retained users get reset/known acceptance credentials.
- Work carried out on a **separate git worktree**.

## Acceptance criteria (from spec Success Criteria)

- [ ] 100% of spaces/users/orgs/memberships in a provisioned acceptance dataset trace to an approved selection entry; any untraceable entity rejects the run.
- [ ] A freshly provisioned acceptance environment starts and every selected space opens with 0 broken-reference/missing-entity errors.
- [ ] Running twice from the same source + selection produces equivalent (idempotent) datasets.
- [ ] A reviewer can produce a first approved selection and provision a working acc environment within one working day, and refresh it in a single re-run.
- [ ] 100% of production content not covered by the selection is excluded and reported; no path for unclassified content to reach acceptance.
- [ ] Every run yields an audit report confirming exactly what was included and why.
- [ ] 0 real personal identifiers remain in substituted fields (name/email); the leak scan rejects any residual.
- [ ] A given source user maps to the identical synthetic identity across runs, and 100% of their memberships/ownership links resolve (no substitution-induced breakage).

## Affected repos (provisional — confirmed at /speckit-plan)

- `server` (owns the entity model / referential closure)
- `infrastructure-operations` (owns the acceptance environment + run surface)

---

Workspace spec: `agents-hq/specs/028-acc-db-derivation/` (`workspace#028-acc-db-derivation`). Single source of truth for this feature.
t: Acc data setup: database derived from production (re-runnable, allowlist-only)

## Description
As a Space visitor or portfolio manager,
I want to filter and search Space listings by Classification values,
So that I can find all Spaces that work on a specific topic (e.g. SDG 13) without scanning every Space manually, and build reliable reports across a portfolio.

**Part of epic: #1985 (Classifications)**

Today, Classifications capture structured metadata on Spaces but offer no way to discover Spaces by that metadata inside the platform. Visitors and reporting users must either scan manually or query the API directly. This story adds in-platform filtering so the structured values become a first-class discovery tool.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A user can filter a Space listing by one or more Classification values (e.g. "SDG 13 · Climate Action")
- [ ] Multiple values within the **same** classification combine with **OR** — a Space matching any of them qualifies
- [ ] Values across **different** classifications combine with **AND** — a Space must satisfy each classification's sub-filter (e.g. *(SDG 13 OR SDG 14) AND (Language: Dutch)*)
- [ ] Filtering operates on the **stable structured value identifiers**, not freeform text — 100% of Spaces carrying a value are returned, with 0 false matches from lookalike Tags
- [ ] Filtering **ignores the display setting** — a Space matches whether the classification is shown or hidden (display governs rendering only)
- [ ] Classification labels and value labels are added to the **search index** so free-text search can also surface Spaces by classification content
- [ ] Filtering by a value that no Space carries returns an empty result, not an error

## Additional Context

- Brings `reporting-orchestration` into scope for search index template changes.
- The structured data shape shipped in the base Classifications iteration already supports querying by stable value id — no data-model migration needed.
- The exact filter UX (sidebar facets, tag-style chips, dropdown) is to be designed; the interaction should feel consistent with existing Space listing filters.
- Deferred requirements carried forward from the base spec: was FR-019, FR-019a, FR-019b, FR-020, SC-009.
- Workspace spec: `agents-hq/specs/024-classifications/spec.md` — "Deferred — follow-on scope" section.
t: Filter and search Spaces by Classification value

## Gap

MCP session revalidation (shipped in `workspace#038`, story #1984) re-checks the **credential** on each request but never the **principal**, and `UserService.deleteUser` has no cascade to `mcp_api_key`. So a user who is deleted, or whose roles are stripped, keeps serving from an already-established MCP session — with their cached `ActorContext` — until the transport closes or the pod restarts.

Found by the adversarial security review of #1984 (`sec-server-1`, high). The risk was **explicitly accepted** to ship #1984; this issue is the agreed follow-up.

### Why #1984 did not close this

#1984 contains a leaked **key**: revoking a key ends its sessions on the next request (verified live — a revoked key's established session gets `401` + `-32001 "Session credential is no longer valid"` and the session is destroyed). It does not contain a leaked **account**, and never claimed to. But an operator reading "contain a leaked key" during an offboarding could reasonably assume account deletion has the same effect. It does not.

## Scope

**Server**

- Extend `UserService.deleteUser`'s post-commit revocation block to revoke (`isActive = false`) every `mcp_api_key` row for the deleted user, writing the matching `KEY_REVOKED` audit rows with `initiatorRole = SYSTEM`. Place it alongside the existing `oidcSessionRevocationService.revokeAllForSub` leg so a rolled-back deletion does not revoke.
- Make session revalidation confirm the bound **principal** still resolves, not just that the key row is usable — rebuild `session.actorContext` via `ActorContextService.buildForUser` / `buildForActor` rather than trusting the cached context.
- Tests against the deletion transaction: deletion revokes the user's keys; a rolled-back deletion does not; an established session for a deleted user is refused on its next request.

### Related

- Depends on the surface added by #1984 (`McpApiKeyService.revokeOwnApiKey` / `adminRevokeApiKey`, `McpApiKeyAuditService`).
- Same `deleteUser` change carries the GDPR erasure finding `sec-server-6` (medium): `mcp_api_key` rows carrying `lastUsedFromIp` — personal data — currently survive user deletion with no erasure path. Handle both in one change.
- Evidence: `agents-hq` → `specs/038-mcp-api-key-management/forge/review-results.md`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Deleting a user revokes all their MCP API keys in the same transaction boundary as the rest of the deletion, with audit rows attributing the action to the system.
- [ ] A deletion that rolls back leaves the keys untouched.
- [ ] An established MCP session belonging to a deleted or role-stripped user is refused on its next request, not on transport close.
- [ ] Personal data on `mcp_api_key` rows (`lastUsedFromIp`) does not outlive the account — either erased at deletion or covered by a documented, enforced retention window (closes `sec-server-6`).
t: [Platform] MCP sessions: revalidate the principal + cascade key revocation on user deletion

## Gap

`McpApiKeyStrategy.extractClientIp` derives the stored `lastUsedFromIp` from the **leftmost** entry of the client-supplied `X-Forwarded-For` header:

```ts
// src/services/mcp-server/auth/mcp-api-key.strategy.ts
private extractClientIp(request: IncomingMessage): string | undefined {
  const forwarded = request.headers['x-forwarded-for'];
  if (forwarded) {
    const ips = typeof forwarded === 'string' ? forwarded : forwarded[0];
    return ips?.split(',')[0]?.trim();   // <- fully caller-controlled
  }
  return request.socket?.remoteAddress;
}
```

That extraction is **pre-existing and unchanged** — it is byte-identical on `develop`. What changed in `workspace#038` (story #1984) is that the value is now **published** to the key's owner and to platform admins as the key's "last used from" source address, i.e. as forensic evidence.

Found by the adversarial security review of #1984 (`sec-server-2`, high). The risk was **explicitly accepted** to ship #1984; this issue is the agreed follow-up.

### Why it matters

The holder of a leaked key controls the evidence shown during the incident that key causes. An attacker sets `X-Forwarded-For` to the victim's own office egress IP on every call; the user and the reviewing admin see only familiar addresses in the keys card, conclude the usage is legitimate, and leave the key active. The field exists to support exactly that judgement call, and it is the one input an attacker can forge.

### Why #1984 did not fix it

A correct fix needs the trust-proxy-resolved client IP, which depends on Traefik's `forwardedHeaders.trustedIPs` — an `infrastructure-operations` change. Architect decision **A-06** for #1984 explicitly scoped infra-ops out. The alternative (dropping the field) is a spec change: `lastUsedFromIp` is named in the story and in FR-008/FR-032.

## Scope

Pick one of two directions — the second is the coordinator's recommendation if the edge work cannot be scheduled promptly.

**A. Pin the edge and resolve honestly (preferred long-term)**
- `infrastructure-operations`: set `forwardedHeaders.trustedIPs` on the Traefik entrypoint so `X-Forwarded-For` is only trusted from known hops.
- `server`: derive the address from the Express `trust proxy`-resolved value (`req.ip`, or the rightmost untrusted hop when the trusted-proxy count is known); validate it as an IP literal before persisting.

**B. Stop publishing it until A lands (recommended interim)**
- Remove `lastUsedFromIp` from `IMcpApiKey` and from both list projections (self + admin), keeping the column internal.
- A forensic field whose subject controls its value is worse than no field: it actively invites the "familiar IP, must be fine" conclusion in the incident it exists to serve. `lastUsedAt` still answers "is this key in use?", which is the load-bearing question.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No surface presents a caller-controllable value as the source address of key usage.
- [ ] If the address is shown at all, it is derived from a trusted-proxy-resolved client IP and validated as an IP literal.
- [ ] If the address is withheld pending edge work, the keys card and the admin surface remain useful for the identify-then-revoke workflow (`lastUsedAt` and status still present).
- [ ] The choice is recorded in the ADR for the MCP API key lifecycle contract (`docs/decisions/0008-mcp-api-key-lifecycle-contract.md`).

### Related

- Follow-up to #1984 (`workspace#038-mcp-api-key-management`).
- Evidence: `agents-hq` → `specs/038-mcp-api-key-management/forge/review-results.md`.
t: [Platform] MCP keys: lastUsedFromIp is caller-controlled — stop publishing it as forensic evidence

## Description
Reorganise the Alkemio Forum from seven overlapping categories to four clearer ones: Releases, Newsletter, Tips & Tricks, Q&A. The work happens in five staged steps: add the new categories, enable admins to reassign posts to other categories (currently disabled), review and reorganise all existing content, remove obsolete posts, delete the old categories.

## Goal
Supports the wider communication ecosystem work - giving each communication channel a distinct, clearly differentiated role. Also supports the CX engagement.

## Hypothesis
Fewer, clearer categories will make the Forum easier to navigate, post in, and search - reducing user confusion and increasing engagement. Leading indicators: no misfiled posts, increased activity in Tips & Tricks and Q&A over 3–6 months; easier curation for admins, users can articulate what each category is for.

## Must have scope

Development:
- Four new categories added (Releases, Newsletter, Tips & Tricks, Q&A)
- Admins can change the category of an existing post
- Newsletter is admin category similar to Releases
- Order of the categories - Releases, Newsletter, Tips & Tricks, Q & A - then all the other categories.

## Goal

Establish a first-class **agentic playground** in Alkemio where stochastic AI processes can explore and produce work inside a deterministic, revocable trust boundary.

The durable work and its audit history survive termination of the sandbox. Only the agent's capability and ephemeral execution environment are disposable.

> **Probabilistic creation. Deterministic governance.**

### Primary job to be done

As a Space steward, I want to grant an AI bounded, revocable access to a persistent set of work, so that it can explore and collaborate without gaining ambient platform authority, while I retain deterministic control over what it can observe, change, and publish.

## Working domain model

### Work Unit

A durable, first-class working set, initially modelled as a work-mode `CalloutsSet` with objective, artifacts, provenance, review/publication state, and a stable identity.

- Owns the callouts and contributions produced during the work.
- Remains available to people after agent access is terminated.
- Can have zero or more sandbox instances over its lifetime.
- Is surfaced in its parent Space through a callout-like card or portal; that card is not itself the trust boundary.

### Sandbox

A disposable **trust envelope** granting explicitly admitted agent identities scoped access to a Work Unit.

It defines:

- admitted agent identities and provider/data-classification policy;
- permitted operations and tools;
- the Work Unit content available by default;
- explicit read-only or snapshot external inputs;
- egress and publication rules;
- expiry and a revocable trust epoch;
- the agent runs performed under that grant.

Terminating a sandbox revokes capabilities and destroys ephemeral credentials, caches, and runtime state. It does **not** delete the Work Unit, its artifacts, provenance, or audit history. Reopening agent access creates a new sandbox identity and trust epoch.

### Agent Run

Each run is an independently persisted and auditable state machine. A run is an attempt against the Work Unit; it is not the Work Unit itself.

Indicative lifecycle:

```text
queued → running ⇄ awaiting_input
             └── proposing → validating
                              ├── completed
                              ├── failed
                              └── cancelled
```

The stochastic agent may emit intents and candidate outcomes. It cannot directly declare protected transitions such as approval or publication.

### Audit ledger

An append-only ledger references the Work Unit, Sandbox, Run, machine/policy version, initiating actor, permitted context and tools, transitions, mutations, proposed outcomes, approvals, revocation, and publication. It survives sandbox termination.

## Deterministic trust contract

The platform must enforce, server-side and fail-closed:

```text
capabilities(tool invocation)
  ⊆ capabilities(run)
  ⊆ capabilities(sandbox)
  ⊆ authority(delegating actor)

readSet(run)  ⊆ sandbox manifest
writeSet(run) ⊆ Work Unit
externalEffects(run) = ∅ until a permitted approval/publication transition
```

“Everything inside is accessible by default” means everything **owned by the Work Unit** is available to principals admitted to its active sandbox. It does not imply ambient access to the parent Space or to entities discoverable by ID.

The boundary must cover every applicable path, including MCP, GraphQL, search, files, whiteboards/collaborative documents, background jobs, and external fetch or messaging tools. No path may rely solely on UI filtering.

Ordinary retrieved content is untrusted data, not an instruction channel. The Work Unit brief and constraints form a distinct trusted instruction source.

## State-machine approach

Use versioned, server-authoritative XState statecharts as the executable lifecycle contracts. Client state machines may render and coordinate the experience, but cannot be authoritative.

Indicative Sandbox lifecycle:

```text
provisioning → active ⇄ suspended
                  ├── expiring → terminated
                  ├── revoking → terminated
                  └── compromised → revoked
```

Entering a security-relevant state must have real capability effects. State-transition and audit persistence must be atomic; external effects must be idempotent and safely queued. Unknown states, unknown events, stale trust epochs, and invalid machine versions fail closed.

## Candidate child stories

1. **Durable Work Unit foundation** — work-mode CalloutsSet, stable identity, Space projection, and human access after sandbox termination.
2. **Sandbox capability envelope** — create, suspend, resume, expire, revoke, terminate, and recreate scoped agent access.
3. **Deterministic Agent Run execution** — versioned per-run statechart, guards, recovery, and transition ledger.
4. **Cross-surface containment** — fail-closed scope enforcement across MCP, GraphQL, search, file and collaboration surfaces.
5. **Trusted context construction** — owned content, explicit external mounts/snapshots, provenance, and instruction/data separation.
6. **Review and controlled publication** — agents propose; guarded or human-approved transitions determine what may leave the Work Unit.
7. **Sandbox and audit UX** — create, observe, suspend, terminate, recreate, inspect runs, and review retained evidence.
8. **Agent-runtime adoption** — integrate the Web AI Assistant, Virtual Contributors, and external MCP clients without granting ambient authority.

## First thin vertical slice

A Space steward creates one Work Unit, admits one agent through one sandbox, and starts one run. The agent can read and write Work Unit content but cannot resolve, read, mutate, or invoke effects outside the sandbox manifest. Terminating the sandbox invalidates access on the next operation while preserving all work and an audit record sufficient to reconstruct the run's authorized context, transitions, tool activity, and outcome.

This slice should remain feature-gated until every exposed access path in its declared tool surface is covered by the containment contract.

## Epic success criteria

- A Work Unit and its artifacts survive termination and recreation of agent sandboxes.
- Every agent operation is attributable to exactly one Work Unit, Sandbox, and Run.
- No run can acquire capabilities beyond both its sandbox and delegating actor.
- Attempts to access an entity outside the sandbox manifest fail regardless of knowledge of its identifier.
- Suspension, expiry, revocation, and termination bind on the next operation.
- Protected transitions and all boundary-crossing effects are deterministically guarded and auditable.
- Reviewers can determine what an agent was allowed to see, what it did, what it proposed, and what was approved or published.
- Sandbox deletion removes ephemeral access and runtime state while retaining durable work and audit evidence.

## Non-goals

- Proving that model reasoning or generated content is correct, truthful, or harmless.
- Treating a client-side state machine or UI visibility rule as a security boundary.
- Giving sandbox agents the ambient permissions of a Space member.
- Replacing the existing Web AI Assistant trust-boundary hardening epic; this is a reusable platform primitive consumed by that and other agent experiences.

## Relationships

- Parent: #1876
- Related trust-boundary hardening: #1948
- Related assistant MVP: #1900
- Related MCP API-key lifecycle: #1984
t: Safe Spaces for AI — agentic work sandboxes

This work is split from [#2038 — Cluster migration follow-up](https://github.com/alkem-io/alkemio/issues/2038). Acceptance-v3 needs its own external dead-man heartbeat for the scheduled backup monitor. It must not reuse the production endpoint, credential, identity or alert state.

## Goal

## Problem

The delivery workspace (agents-hq) plus the 18 sibling repos hold **~330 SDD specs — 27,897 markdown sections** of institutional memory: architecture decisions, council dissent, verified facts, risk registers, forge run ledgers, ADRs. None of it is searchable except by grep, and grep requires already knowing the vocabulary — the failure mode is precisely *not remembering which spec discussed X*.

Separately, forge runs write structured economics (per-invocation provider/model/token/cost records) that are computed in-memory and never persisted — there is no cost time-series across runs.

## What was built (first increment, shipped)

`.scripts/spec-index.py` in agents-hq — a single SQLite+FTS5 database (`.index/`, gitignored, rebuildable in ~3s), stdlib-only, indexing:

- **Prose** → FTS5 (BM25, porter stemming), chunked by markdown section, with provenance (origin repo, spec id, file, heading, git HEAD at index time): workspace specs + ADRs + forge ledgers/handoff bodies, all 18 sibling repos' `specs/` trees (read-only), and the operator memory dir.
- **State** → plain SQL tables: handoff frontmatter (227 rows), invocation metadata sidecars, `run.json` summaries. Queried by structure (`SUM`/`GROUP BY`), never by similarity — persisted economics for the first time.

Verified against real recall questions ("which spec discussed session revalidation on revoke", "who objected to IAuthorizable promotion and why") — both resolve to the exact `verified-facts.md` / adjudication sections.

## Remaining work

- [x] **MCP tool** so agent sessions (Claude Code / Codex) can query the index directly instead of shelling out
- [x] **Rebuild trigger** — hook or cron so the index tracks spec merges without manual `rebuild`
- [x] **Spec-dir structure**: decide the `specs/` layout convention the index should canonicalize (e.g. splitting machine evidence from prose — ~13 MB of the 20 MB tree is Trivy/SBOM blobs, already excluded from indexing)
- [ ] **Embedding upgrade (optional, later)**: add a vector column for semantic recall beyond BM25; chunking + provenance schema already supports it. Note: the platform ES cluster (8.17.1 basic, `ml.available: false`) cannot host inference — external embeddings only.
- [x] **`verified-facts.md` as a mandatory forge artifact**, commit-pinned, so ground-truth claims are indexable and staleness-detectable (motivated by the 038 run's stale-clone grep incident)

## Context

Workspace: `agents-hq` (`.scripts/spec-index.py`). Related: workspace#038 forge run ledger (the recall failures that motivated this), ADR: `docs/decisions/0008-institutional-memory-index.md` (agents-hq PR #98). All increments except the optional embedding upgrade landed in [agents-hq#98](https://github.com/alkem-io/agents-hq/pull/98); the embedding column stays deferred with its trigger condition (observed lexical-miss failures, not a date) recorded in the ADR.

**Epic.** Close the gap between the Virtual Contributor's *well-governed* RAG (strong privacy-egress discipline, provider-approval gates, audit-grade delivery) and *demonstrably world-class* RAG (retrieval quality that is measured, corpus that is fresh, evaluation that can be trusted, operations that don't erode user trust). The thesis of this epic: 11 review rounds of `workspace#050` perfected everything *around* retrieval while the retrieval-quality question itself stayed unanswered.

Origin: 2026-08-16 adversarial architecture review of the VC RAG stack (during the `workspace#050-vc-two-stage-retrieval` forge runs), grilled against 2025-26 industry RAG practice.

## The six deltas

**1. Retrieval efficacy is unproven.** RG-05 (paired flat vs two-stage evaluation on the same case set) is still an open gate. On develop, two-stage was effectively a no-op (single summary at CHUNK_SIZE=9000; `query()` had no `where=` filter — vc#19 prerequisites). Every RAG story under epic #1818/#1819 shipped with a premise later refuted by execution.
→ *Deliverable: run RG-05 honestly; ship precision@k / groundedness / abstention-on-out-of-corpus numbers per release. Be prepared for "flat was fine."*

**2. The evaluation harness manufactured false confidence.** The workspace#050 ADR history records: synthetic positive RAGAS evidence, whole-frame metric extraction, zero-success aggregates labeled complete, invalid aggregates labeled complete, coercive comparison imports.
→ *Deliverable: human-labeled golden dataset with inter-annotator agreement; eval-harness regression tests; online user-feedback signal.*

**3. The corpus is stale by design.** Re-ingestion is a manual human gate; deploys never rewrite existing collections. Round-11 finding spec-vc-1 proved the consequence: a privacy fix inert on exactly the persisted (pre-workspace#043) corpus users query.
→ *Deliverable: event-driven / incremental ingestion; per-space ingestion-freshness observability ("when was this collection last ingested" answerable in one query).*

**4. Retrieval architecture is below 2025-26 table stakes.** No cross-encoder rerank stage; structure-blind ~9000-char chunking; one query-rewrite LLM call as the whole query-understanding layer; a prior round found live retrieval bypassing the selected hybrid identity.
→ *Deliverable: measure (don't assume) reranking, contextual/late chunking, and parent-document retrieval against the RG-05 baseline; adopt what wins.*

**5. The operational floor is below the architectural ceiling.** Live on develop: failed `ack()` → duplicate error reply to the member + a third full plugin run (rides on vc PR #108). Ten feature PRs merge clean alone but conflict in sequence (86 hunks). Users experience duplicate replies, not embedding choices.
→ *Deliverable: message-lifecycle correctness (ack/redelivery/dedupe) verified under fault injection; PR-pileup burn-down.*

**6. Keep the strength: privacy-egress discipline.** The provider-boundary story (stable-ID excision, endpoint-free logging, RG-05P approval gate) is ahead of most industry RAG deployments — this epic must not regress it while moving fast on 1–5.

**Explicitly NOT in scope:** workspace#050 remediation itself (in flight, forge run) · Web AI Assistant RAG (#1948–#1952 family) · ingestion engine re-platforming beyond incremental ingestion.

Related: #1818 (VC quality epic) · #1815 (program epic) · virtual-contributor#19 (two-stage retrieval story) · `workspace#050-vc-two-stage-retrieval`.
t: World-class RAG delta — Virtual Contributor retrieval quality

**Blocks formal discharge of RG-05 for `virtual-contributor#19` / `workspace#050-vc-two-stage-retrieval`.** Delta #2 of the World-class RAG epic ("the evaluation harness manufactured false confidence") — this time the harness failed *closed*, which is the improvement, but it still cannot produce a verdict.

## Symptom

`python -m evaluation compare <flat> <hier>` refuses:

```
ValueError: Evaluation comparison requires failure-free runs
    at evaluation/report.py:314 compute_comparison
```

Both runs report `success_count: 0`, `failure_count: 15`, and every case carries:

```
error: "Evaluation metric must be within inclusive [0, 1]"
```

## Root cause: RAGAS `AnswerRelevancy` returns `nan` in this environment

Retrieval and answering are **fine** — all 30 cases across both arms produced correct answers with the right documents. The failure is purely in metric scoring. Isolating one case:

```
faithfulness                            1.0     OK
llm_context_precision_without_reference 0.9999  OK
context_recall                          1.0     OK
answer_relevancy                        nan     <-- fails the run
```

with RAGAS emitting internally:

```
Exception raised in Job[1]: TypeError(unsupported operand type(s) for +=: 'dict' and 'dict')
```

Environment: `ragas 0.4.3`, evaluator embeddings configured in `evaluation/cli.py:107-111` as `langchain_openai.OpenAIEmbeddings` pointed at the Scaleway endpoint (`https://api.scaleway.ai/v1`, `qwen3-embedding-8b`). The embeddings themselves are healthy (`embed_query` returns a 4096-float vector); the incompatibility is inside RAGAS's `AnswerRelevancy` strictness/aggregation path.

The resulting `nan` correctly trips `finite_unit_metric()` (`evaluation/report.py:25-34`) — the fail-closed guard built for risk **R-34** ("non-finite or out-of-domain metrics authorize false RG-05 evidence"). **The product validation is working as designed.** The problem is that one unscoreable metric of four fails the *entire case*, and 15 failed cases block the comparison the gate requires.

## Impact

RG-05 cannot be formally satisfied **in either direction** until this is fixed. The gate's pass condition was measured out-of-band by scoring `context_precision` alone over the two persisted runs (honest supplementary evidence, not a framework-computed zero-failure comparison) and was found **not met** — see `alkem-io/virtual-contributor#121`. So the immediate decision is unblocked, but the gate record is not.

## Suggested directions

1. **Diagnose the RAGAS/embeddings incompatibility** — pin a known-good RAGAS version, migrate to the non-deprecated `ragas.metrics.collections` API (0.4.3 already warns that `ragas.metrics.AnswerRelevancy` and `LangchainLLMWrapper` are deprecated), or use a RAGAS-compatible embeddings client for the evaluator only (the *pipeline* embeddings need not change).
2. **Separate metric-level failure from case-level failure.** A case whose retrieval and answer succeeded but where one metric is unscoreable is not the same as a case that failed. Record the metric as unavailable, keep the case's other metrics, and let the gate decide whether its own pass metric is present — rather than discarding four good measurements because a fourth is broken. (Design change: must not weaken R-34 — an out-of-domain value must still never *become* evidence.)
3. **Add a harness self-test** that scores a fixed known-good sample and asserts all four metrics land in `[0, 1]` — so an evaluator-stack incompatibility is caught in CI rather than mid-gate.

## Reproduction

```bash
# in the virtual-contributor worktree, with evaluator env configured
poetry run python -c "
from evaluation.metrics import create_metrics
from langchain_mistralai import ChatMistralAI
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
from ragas import evaluate, EvaluationDataset, SingleTurnSample
# ... build one sample from a persisted evaluations/*.json case ...
print(evaluate(dataset=EvaluationDataset(samples=[sample]), metrics=create_metrics(chat, emb)).scores)
# -> [{'faithfulness': 1.0, 'answer_relevancy': nan, ...}]
"
```

Related: `alkem-io/virtual-contributor#121` (the product defect RG-05 surfaced), `virtual-contributor#19`, `workspace#050-vc-two-stage-retrieval`.

## Background

Thorough three-agent research (Aug 2026) into whether Pulumi or another tool could streamline Alkemio infra operations. Conclusion: **no IaC tool rewrite is needed; the operational gap is in the Kubernetes deploy layer, not the cloud provisioning layer.**

### Verdict

| Idea | Verdict | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Adopt Pulumi | ❌ No | Architecturally incompatible with inert-artifact security model; downgrades Scaleway provider; optimizes wrong axis |
| Adopt Flux CD + fix drift-check | ✅ Yes | 3-5 weeks, low risk, closes 100% of operational pain |
| Add CI to provisioning | ✅ Yes, optional | Moderate lift, closes provisioning-visibility gap |
| Terraform modularization | ✅ Yes, post-roadmap | 2-3 days, code-representation wins |

### Why NOT Pulumi

1. **Security model inversion** - 2157-line static validator proves v3 roots are understandable without credentials; Pulumi programs need live creds to evaluate
2. **Scaleway provider downgrade** - first-party v2.81.0 (Scaleway-published) vs community v1.54.0 (two-person bus factor)
3. **Wrong axis** - 3916 lines TF/59 commits/yr vs 154k lines Kustomize/739 commits/yr; Pulumi optimizes 2.5%

### Top 4 pain points (of 16 ranked from repo audit)

- **P6** - 7 Helm releases outside GitOps; alert rules silently inactive without manual helm upgrade
- **P5** - Drift gate switched off in both environments
- **P4** - Server image tag in 4 files (split-brain deploy risk)
- **P3** - 6869 lines of bash validators because configs are not typed

### What Flux adds

| Capability | Current | Flux |
|---|---|---|
| Orphan detection | Blind | Continuous reconciliation |
| Helm GitOps | Manual x7 | HelmRelease CRD |
| Image automation | Hand-edited | ImageRepository auto-commit |
| Auto-rollback | None | Progressive delivery |

### Roadmap (5 weeks)

- **Week 1-2:** S1 Re-enable drift gate (merge fix/2541, delete continue-on-error)
- **Week 1-3:** S2 Flux Helm GitOps (install Flux, migrate 7 charts to HelmRelease)
- **Week 3-4:** S3 Flux image automation (ImageRepository + ImagePolicy for all app images)
- **Week 4-5 (optional):** CI on provisioning (terraform plan on PR)

Surfaced 2026-08-18 while assessing what it would take to point an **external agent harness** (OpenClaw / Hermes / Pi-class runtime) at the Alkemio MCP host for a research → convergence workflow.

## Summary

An MCP API key **cannot be minted to be less than its owner**. There are two independent axes on which an agent credential needs narrowing, and both land at the **same enforcement point** in `mcp-server.service.ts`:

| Axis | Question | State today |
|---|---|---|
| **Capability** — *which tools?* | `search_content` only, or everything? | Mechanism **exists** but skips non-assistant callers |
| **Space** — *which spaces?* | only the R&D space, or the platform? | Declared, **not implemented**, fails closed |

This story delivers both, capability first (cheap, high leverage), then space.

## First, what is NOT broken

This is **not an authorization hole**, and the story should not be read as one.

Every MCP path runs the same `AuthorizationService` as GraphQL. Search results are filtered per-entity through `isAccessGranted(…, READ)` — **7 call sites** in `search.result.service.ts`. Write tools delegate to the same domain mutations as GraphQL (e.g. `create_whiteboard_in_space` → `CalloutsSetResolverMutations.createCalloutOnCalloutsSet`, enforcing `CREATE_CALLOUT`).

**A key can never read or write more than its owner.** The gap is only that it cannot be granted *less*.

## The architectural finding — the paths are already ~95% converged

There is **exactly one** `tools/call` handler. Assistant and external MCP callers already share the tool registry, argument validation, every tool implementation, and the per-entity authorization inside each tool. **There is no duplicated tool code to merge.**

```
scopeViolation(scopes, 'tools')                 ← shared
  → argsValidator.validate(…)                   ← shared
  → capabilityGateService.checkToolAllowed(…)   ← ★ the ONLY divergence
  → tool.execute(args, actorContext)            ← shared
```

The entire divergence is four lines in `AssistantCapabilityGateService.checkToolAllowed`:

```ts
const delegation = actorContext.delegationContext;
if (!delegation) {
  // Not an assistant call — no per-tool gate applies here.
  return null;
}
```

An external API-key caller carries no `delegationContext`, so it **skips the gate entirely**. This is not a separate code path — it is a **hole in a shared one**.

### Why the fix is small

The gate already resolves toggles from two sources and then runs identical logic:

- Flow A (delegated) → `user.settings.assistant.enabledCapabilities`
- Flow B (system-invoked) → `virtualAssistant.capabilityGrant`

Both are `IAssistantCapabilityToggle[]`. The interface comment states it outright: *"The same shape backs both the per-user authority grant and the admin grant on the actor."* `isEnabled()` is already generic over the source.

**Convergence = giving an MCP API key a third source of that same array.** `McpApiKey` gains a `capabilityGrant` jsonb column, resolved in `McpApiKeyStrategy` exactly as `scopes` already is (it already rides the request via `mcpApiKeyScopes`). Then one gate, three grant sources, every caller covered.

Absence ⇒ disabled, consistent with the existing rule: *"a new WRITE capability the user has never seen is off by default."*

**Naming consequence:** `AssistantCapabilityGateService` stops being assistant-specific — it becomes the platform capability gate with the assistant as one client. The rename is the honest signal that there is one gate, not an assistant feature.

## Why it matters

- **Blast radius.** A credential handed to an external harness concentrates the owner's whole platform authority in one bearer token in third-party config. Observed concretely: a working prod MCP token sits in plaintext in `~/.claude.json`. For an admin-held key that is the entire platform.
- **`['read','tools']` means every tool, everywhere.** Because the gate skips this caller, there is no way to hand out a key that may only call `search_content` + `create_whiteboard_in_space`.
- **Blocks #1912.** Opening the MCP host at the edge without a narrowing primitive makes every external client an all-or-nothing platform credential.
- **First concrete slice of #2055.** The Safe Spaces trust contract requires `capabilities(tool invocation) ⊆ capabilities(sandbox) ⊆ authority(delegating actor)`. Today the middle term does not exist — a key is the full actor or nothing. Candidate child story 4 ("cross-surface containment") names exactly this.

## Slice 1 — capability scoping (do this first)

- [ ] `McpApiKey.capabilityGrant: IAssistantCapabilityToggle[]` (jsonb, nullable) + migration.
- [ ] `McpApiKeyStrategy` resolves it onto the request alongside `mcpApiKeyScopes`; `McpDelegationStrategy` unaffected.
- [ ] Replace the `if (!delegation) return null` early return with a resolution against the key's grant; absence ⇒ disabled (fail-closed).
- [ ] Rename `AssistantCapabilityGateService` → platform-neutral (e.g. `McpCapabilityGateService`); update the class comment — it now governs three grant sources, not two.
- [ ] Key-creation API accepts an optional capability grant; document that omitting it yields a read-only key.
- [ ] Tests: a key granted only `search_content` is refused `create_whiteboard_in_space`; an ungranted key is refused all tools; assistant Flow A/B behaviour is unchanged (regression).

## Slice 2 — space scoping

`McpApiKeyScope.spaceIds` is declared but unenforced, and `scopeViolation()` fails closed on it:

```ts
if (scopes.some(scope => scope.spaceIds && scope.spaceIds.length > 0)) {
  return 'This API key is restricted to specific spaces (spaceIds), which the MCP server does not yet enforce. Use an unrestricted key.';
}
```

- [ ] Enforce `spaceIds` on **resource reads** and **tool calls**, server-side, fail-closed.
- [ ] Constrain `search_content` to the scoped spaces — search must not become the enumeration bypass (`searchInSpaceFilter` already exists).
- [ ] Decide + document containment for entities reachable by ID but outside scope (resolve-then-deny vs. not-found), and for cross-space resources (templates, platform lookups).
- [ ] Subspace semantics: does scoping to an L0 space include L1/L2 descendants? (Proposal: yes, explicitly documented.)
- [ ] Remove the fail-closed guard in `scopeViolation()` once enforcement lands; keep it until then.
- [ ] Tests across **every** MCP path — tools, resources, search.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A key can be minted that may call only a named subset of the 11 tools; all others are refused fail-closed.
- [ ] A key with `spaceIds: [X]` can read/write within X (and, per decided semantics, its subspaces) and is denied everywhere else — verified across tools, resources, and search.
- [ ] Both checks are enforced server-side at the host boundary, never UI-only, and fail closed on unknown/ambiguous targets.
- [ ] One capability gate serves assistant-delegated, assistant-system-invoked, and external-key callers; no per-caller branch remains.
- [ ] `scopeViolation()` no longer rejects space-scoped keys.
- [ ] Containment semantics documented in the MCP host spec.

## Non-goals / non-overlap

- **Not** short-TTL or delegation-token redesign — that is #1955 (ADR). This narrows the *existing* static-key model and is complementary; it should **not** wait on the ADR.
- **Not** the Safe Spaces sandbox lifecycle (#2055) — no Work Unit, no trust epochs, no run statecharts. This is the capability-narrowing primitive those build on.
- **Not** OAuth2 `client_credentials` (server#6077) or scope→credential mapping (server#6075), though the semantics decided here should inform both.
- **Not** edge exposure (#1912) — but a sensible prerequisite for it.
- **Not** re-opening server#6142, which built the gate for assistant flows; this generalizes it.

## Side findings (not in scope — filed here so they are not lost)

- **#1912 may be stale.** It states `/rest/mcp` has no public Traefik route in acc/prod, but a production MCP session was established from **outside** the cluster on 2026-08-18 (tools + resources listed, a whiteboard read and written). Either a route now exists or it is reachable by a path the issue did not account for. Worth reconciling, since sequencing depends on it.
- **`create_whiteboard_in_space` drops profile metadata.** It hardcodes `framing: { profile: { displayName } }`, while `CreateProfileInput` supports `description`, `tags`, `tagsets`, and `referencesData`. An agent therefore cannot land a tagged, referenced, findable artifact. ~20-line passthrough; likely its own story.
- **"Immediately searchable" is not true today.** Search ingest is `ingestFromScratch` — full reindex + alias swap, triggered by an admin mutation; there is no incremental single-document index path. A newly created whiteboard is not findable via `search_content` until the next full ingest. Tags/profile work immediately; full-text lags. Material to any agent flow that uses search as a novelty check.

**Repos:** `server` (+ workspace spec)

**Related:** #2055 (parent epic — child story 4) · #1955 (delegation-token ADR) · #1912 (edge exposure) · #1876 (assistant/agent platform epic) · server#6142 (built the gate) · server#6077 · server#6075

🤖 Drafted from a 2026-08-18 code-level review of the MCP auth, gating, and scoping path.
t: [Platform] Least-privilege MCP agent credentials: one capability gate for all callers + spaceIds scoping

## Description
Push notifications are the highest-value native capability called out in #1737 ("it's the feature that could justify why we submit our website in the stores") and were explicitly deferred as a scoped follow-up in the app-store wrapping spike (#2024). Real-time notification delivery already exists for the PWA via web-push (#1797); this epic extends that to native push (APNs/FCM) for the wrapped iOS/Android apps currently in internal testing.

## Goal
Give users working push notifications in the wrapped native app, and validate that push notifications alone move the needle on the "minimum functionality" store-approval risk flagged in #2024.

## Hypothesis
Both stores reject apps that only present a website, and each review round trip costs days. Push notifications are the most likely to justify the app's existence to a reviewer, and they're the most likely to actually drive repeat opens once installed.

## Must have scope
(AI-written, needs to be checked by developer)
- [ ] Decide the push service: native APNs/FCM directly, a unified sender (e.g. FCM for both platforms), or a push feature built into the app-wrapping vendor (open item from #1737 — depends on confirming which wrapper tool #2024 used)
- [ ] Native device registration: capture APNs/FCM (or vendor) push token per user/device
- [ ] Backend: store device tokens and extend the existing notification dispatch (currently web-push/VAPID per #1797) to also fan out to native push
- [ ] Reuse existing notification preference model (opt-in/out) from #1797 rather than building a new one
- [ ] In-app permission prompt UX (native push permission dialog, timed sensibly rather than asked cold on first launch)
- [ ] Tapping a notification opens the relevant space/conversation in-app (deep link on tap — minimal routing needed even without full universal-links support)
- [ ] Manual test pass on the existing TestFlight / Play internal testing tracks (#2024)

## Stakeholders


## Additional Context
Relates to #1801 (Matrix-native messaging — reworks the backend notification event plane) and #1737 (native app epic).

## Privacy and data protection — for the refinement

Surfaced while updating the legal pages for the mobile app (website-alkemio#232). Two things belong in this epic rather than in a privacy policy PR, because the disclosure has to follow the supplier decision rather than precede it.

**There is already a gap today, independent of native push.** Web push is live: `subscribeToPushNotifications` stores `endpoint`, `auth`, `p256dh`, `userAgent`, `status` and `lastActiveDate` per device, tied to a user account. The privacy policy mentions push nowhere — there is no row for it in the processing table and no paragraph describing it. That is device-level personal data being processed without a stated purpose or legal basis. It should be fixed whether or not native push ever ships, and the wording is cheap once someone confirms the retention and opt-in model. The draft mobile PR deliberately contains no push text at all, so nothing is blocked on this.

**The push-service decision in scope above is also a sub-processor decision**, and the options are not equivalent:

- *Direct to APNs and FCM from our own notification service* — no third-party SDK, tokens stay in our database. Apple and Google become transport sub-processors. Unavoidable on both platforms, and a transfer outside the EEA in both cases.
- *A vendor (OneSignal, Airship, Braze, AWS SNS, or a wrapper's built-in push)* — these sit **on top of** APNs and FCM. They add a processor; they do not remove Google or Apple.
- *UnifiedPush* — genuinely avoids Google on Android, but requires the user to install a separate distributor app, which rules it out for a public store release.
- On iOS there is no choice at all: APNs is the only transport.

**One decision worth taking here rather than afterwards:** send data-only payloads and render the notification text on the device. Then the transport only ever sees a device token and routing metadata, never who said what to whom. That is a far easier position to describe in the privacy policy than a payload that carries message content through a third party, and it is much cheaper to design in than to retrofit.

**Useful context for the "are there alternatives to Firebase" question raised in review:** web push on Chrome already routes through Google's browser push service, without Alkemio holding a Firebase project or API key. That is a materially different kind of involvement than FCM as our own processor. How it should be characterised is a question for the DPO.


### Wording ready to apply for the existing web-push gap

Not applied anywhere yet — drafted so the refinement can approve or reject it rather than start from a blank page. It covers only web push as it works today; native push wording follows the service decision above.

Proposed row for the processing table in section 4 of the Privacy Policy:

| Purpose | Personal data category | Legal justification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Push notification delivery | Activity and Behavioural, Technical Identifiers | Consent |

Proposed paragraph to sit under that table:

> **Push notifications.** If You choose to receive push notifications, Your browser or device creates a subscription for that device and We store it so that We can deliver those notifications to You. The subscription consists of the address Your browser gives Us for delivery, the keys needed to encrypt the message, Your browser's user agent string, and the date on which the subscription was last active. We do not use it for any purpose other than delivering the notifications You have asked for. You can withdraw Your consent at any time in Your notification settings or in Your browser, which stops further notifications being sent to that device.

Two deliberate omissions, both worth a decision in the refinement:

- **It says nothing about how long a subscription is kept or when it is removed.** server#5961 reports that unsubscribed subscriptions are returned as disabled rather than removed, so any claim about deletion would not currently be true. Once that bug is fixed the paragraph can say what actually happens.
- **Consent is stated as the basis** because the subscription is only created after the user accepts the browser permission prompt. Worth confirming that matches how the opt-in preference model from #1797 actually behaves.

Related: server#5951 reports that a subscription can be created with empty `endpoint` and `auth` values, which is a data-quality problem in the same table.
t: App Notifications

## What this is

Before the browser can talk to Synapse directly, it needs its own Matrix login. This task defines exactly how that login happens without the user seeing a second sign-in screen, proves it works on a test environment, and gets the security trade-offs signed off.

Part of epic alkem-io/alkemio#1801 (gate 1 of 10). The code that implements it is alkem-io/client-web#10157.

## In plain terms

A user already signed in to Alkemio opens chat. In a hidden frame the browser asks Synapse to log it in; Synapse asks our identity chain (Hydra → oidc-service → Kratos) "who is this?", gets the answer, and hands the browser a one-time token. The browser swaps that for a Matrix access token and a refresh token and keeps them in its own storage (IndexedDB). The Alkemio login cookie itself is never sent to Synapse and never doubles as a Matrix credential.

## What we had to decide (all decided; recorded in the spec)

- Where the tokens live in the browser: plain values in a per-user IndexedDB namespace, wiped on logout (decided 2026-09-03; encrypting them or keeping them at the edge were evaluated and rejected).
- Only one tab syncs at a time (Web Locks); the others follow.
- The refresh token now lives 48 hours instead of 5 minutes so an idle browser can resume silently. Side effect: a crashed browser's session stays revivable for up to 48 hours. Named "R-10" and accepted with eyes open.
- There is no Content-Security-Policy anywhere today; adding one is alkem-io/infrastructure-operations#2590.

## Done when

- [ ] A sequence diagram shows every hop between browser, Alkemio, Synapse, Hydra and Kratos, and where each credential lives.
- [x] A signed-in user gets a Matrix session with no second prompt.
- [x] Expired or revoked sessions, logout, switching users, several tabs, and users without a Matrix account all fail safely (no wrong identity, no leftover data).
- [x] The Alkemio cookie and Synapse's client secret are never reachable from JavaScript.
- [x] Token storage and single-tab sync are written down as an approved decision.
- [x] The proof was run on a non-production environment (sandbox, 2026-09-06) and attached here with rollback notes.

## Still open here

Security review sign-off on the three named trade-offs (browser-held tokens, the 48-hour window, no CSP yet). It gates turning the feature on for real users, not the proof. ADR 0009 acceptance rides alkem-io/agents-hq#107.

## Not in this task

Reading or sending messages from the browser (#10158, #10159), end-to-end encryption, federation, changing who may talk to whom.

## Read more

Spec: https://github.com/alkem-io/agents-hq/tree/053-matrix-browser-session/specs/053-matrix-browser-session (PR alkem-io/agents-hq#122)
t: Define and prove the Matrix/OIDC browser session contract

## Outcome

After the Matrix-native web client has a proven direct media path, retire the #1946 web-facing attachment proxy surfaces that no longer have consumers. Preserve the Synapse storage-provider/file-service byte path and any backend ingestion needed for Alkemio authorization, document accounting, notifications, audit, or reconciliation.

Predecessor: alkem-io/alkemio#1801. This is a post-epic follow-up and does not
block #1801 from being completed.

This is a post-epic retirement slice, not a prerequisite for initially integrating `matrix-js-sdk`. It must not start merely because #1946 has rolled out or direct text messaging works.

## Candidate retirement scope

- Client GraphQL attachment send/read projection that is replaced by Matrix media APIs.
- Server attachment message mutations, timeline projection, and read-resolution paths used only by the migrated web client.
- Server → adapter outbound attachment commands used only to upload and emit web-origin media on the client's behalf.
- Adapter file-service fetch, `UploadBytes`, outbound media-event construction, DTO fields, and appservice-ghost `io.alkemio.document_id` handling that have no remaining trusted consumer.
- Feature flags, fallback branches, metrics, tests, and compatibility code whose observation window proves them unused.

The inventory decides the actual deletion set; nothing above is presumed unused without evidence.

## Explicitly retained unless separately replaced

- Synapse media storage provider ↔ file-service byte storage.
- #1996 historical media backfill outcome and Synapse retention/purge ownership.
- Synapse → adapter → server processing required to create/re-home conversation-scoped document rows, attribute uploaders, enforce Alkemio policy, or drive notifications/audit/reconciliation.
- Alkemio conversation and membership authorization.
- Non-web and rollback consumers discovered by the inventory.

## Prerequisite gates

- [ ] #1946 is merged, rolled out, and its as-built behavior is the measured baseline.
- [ ] The #1801 direct-media design is approved, including upload/download, event provenance, document correlation, Alkemio policy/canonicalization, membership-protected retrieval, Element interoperability, and rollback.
- [ ] Supported web attachment sends and reads use Matrix media APIs for the full production cohort.
- [ ] Backend document accounting and notification/audit consumers operate correctly from direct-client media events.
- [ ] #1996 and the production media-storage cutover have completed where still required.
- [ ] The established media proxy remains available until rollback gates are closed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A consumer inventory classifies every #1946 client/server/adapter media surface as removed, retained, or replaced, with an owner and evidence.
- [ ] The migrated web client uploads, emits, receives, and downloads supported attachments through the approved Matrix-native path without using retired GraphQL message transport.
- [ ] Direct media preserves non-member denial, uploader attribution, conversation-scoped document accounting, supported Alkemio policy, and Element interoperability.
- [ ] Normal Matrix clients cannot forge trusted Alkemio document correlation or obtain media outside the approved authorization model.
- [ ] Zero migrated-web use of candidate proxy surfaces is observed for at least 14 consecutive production days after full direct-media adoption.
- [ ] Removing the proxy causes no missing/duplicate media events, broken historical attachments, notification regressions, or orphaned required document records.
- [ ] Rollback and recovery are tested before deletion; removal is separately reviewed and remains behind normal human merge/deployment gates.

## Ownership

Cross-repository retirement involving `client-web`, `server`, and `matrix-adapter`, with `file-service`, infrastructure, security, and QA review. Requires senior Matrix/media and backend ownership; it is not a frontend-only cleanup.
t: Retire the #1946 web media proxy after direct Matrix media cutover

## Description
As an Alkemio account holder
I want every change to my sign-in methods — connecting or disconnecting an identity provider — to be written to the platform audit trail and confirmed to me with a security notification
So that I (and the platform) can detect and react to an unauthorized change to how my account can be accessed, exactly as is already possible for a password change.

## Context

#2079 delivers the **Connected Accounts** section in Security settings (connect / disconnect an identity provider) as a client-only increment. A **password change** already produces both a durable audit record and a security signal to the user; a provider connect/disconnect — which equally changes the set of first-factor credentials that can reach the account — currently produces **neither**.

This gap was accepted deliberately and time-boxed so the client slice could ship first; this story closes it. It was a pre-agreed condition of #2079 that this follow-up is on the board before that work completes.

The likely mechanism already has precedent: the password-changed signal is delivered via a Kratos settings-flow `after` web hook. The same pattern can be applied to the `oidc` method (link/unlink), keeping the user's flow fail-open if the hook is unavailable, matching the password behaviour.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Should write a platform audit entry when a provider is **connected** to an account (actor, provider, timestamp)
- [ ] Should write a platform audit entry when a provider is **disconnected** from an account (actor, provider, timestamp)
- [ ] Should send the account holder a security notification for each **completed** connect and disconnect, naming the provider and when it happened, with guidance for the case where they did not initiate it
- [ ] Should apply to **every** identity provider the platform offers (provider-agnostic; CleverBase included)
- [ ] Should not audit or notify on failed, expired, or abandoned attempts — only on completed changes
- [ ] Should keep the user's settings flow fail-open if the audit/notification hook is unavailable (parity with the password-changed hook behaviour)
- [ ] Should be covered by automated tests for both the audit write and the notification dispatch

## Additional Context

- Epic: #1947 · Delivered UI increment this follows up: #2079 · Decision map: #2060
- Affected areas (expected): server (audit entry + notification dispatch), kratos-webhooks (settings-flow hook for the oidc method), identity configuration (hook wiring)
t: Audit and notify on sign-in method changes (provider connect/disconnect)

## Description
Two external, independent assessment tools currently flag gaps in Alkemio's domain security configuration and vendor-trust/transparency posture:

- **[internet.nl website test](https://internet.nl/site/www.alkem.io)** — `www.alkem.io` currently scores **62%**, failing the IPv6, DNSSEC and HTTPS categories, with a suggestion to improve security headers.
- **[Moral Fabric fingerprint](https://app.moralfabric.org/fingerprint?domain=Alkem.io)** — confirms Alkemio is hosted in the EU (Scaleway, France/Netherlands), but flags that no public legal pages could be found on the domain, and that there is no SPF record (allowing mail spoofing of `alkem.io`). It also notes that staff email (Microsoft 365) and the TLS certificate authority (Let's Encrypt) are US-based providers.

This Epic covers investigating and closing these gaps, to strengthen Alkemio's technical security posture and its public trust/transparency signals — both of which are checked by (potential) partners and hosting organisations evaluating Alkemio as an open, EU-hosted platform.

## Goal
Raise Alkemio's score on both external scanners, to build justified, verifiable trust with users, partners and organisations that use these public, independent tools to vet SaaS vendors before adopting them.

## Hypothesis
Most of the flagged items are configuration-level (DNS, TLS, HTTP headers, legal pages) rather than architectural, so they can be resolved without major engineering effort.

Success is measured by re-running both scans after the fixes land and confirming the flagged items now pass:
- internet.nl score of 62% (2026-08-25) → target 90%+
- Moral Fabric: "no public legal pages found" and "no SPF record" flags resolved

## Must have scope
_Define what is a must-have for launch and in-scope. Keep this section fluid and dynamic until you lock-in priority during planning._

### internet.nl (score 62% as of 2026-08-25)
- [ ] IPv6 — enable IPv6 on the webserver (nameservers already support it)
- [ ] DNSSEC — sign the alkem.io domain
- [ ] HTTPS — enable HSTS; review and tighten the TLS cipher suite configuration
- [ ] Security options — add `Content-Security-Policy` and `X-Content-Type-Options` headers; review `X-Frame-Options` and `Referrer-Policy`; publish a `security.txt`

Wayfinder map for epic #2083. Charted 2026-08-25.

## Destination

A locked set of decisions — every DNS, TLS, HTTP-header and discoverability change fully specified and ready to hand to `/sdd-epic` — such that a re-run of **[internet.nl](https://internet.nl/site/www.alkem.io)** and the **[Moral Fabric fingerprint](https://app.moralfabric.org/fingerprint?domain=Alkem.io)** passes the flagged items. **Decisions only; nothing is applied by this map.** The map is done when nothing is left to decide before that work can be executed.

## Notes

**Domain**: Alkemio's public trust surface — DNS for `alkem.io` (Scaleway DNS, `ns0`/`ns1.dom.scw.cloud`), the app at `alkem.io`/`www.alkem.io` (Scaleway, nginx ingress, wildcard Let's Encrypt cert), and the marketing/legal site at `welcome.alkem.io` (Bunny CDN).

**Scope — three hosts only**: `alkem.io`, `www.alkem.io`, `welcome.alkem.io`. These are what a vendor-vetting scanner touches. API and internal subdomains are out of scope.

**Hard constraint — `alkem-io/alkemio` is a PUBLIC repository.** Never cite private repositories here: no file paths, line numbers, commit SHAs, PR numbers, or verbatim configuration from the infrastructure, orchestration or workspace repos. Findings that require that detail live in internal research notes; refer to them by description only. The *findings themselves* (which controls are missing) are public by design — both scanners publish them to anyone who types the domain, and public transparency is the point of this epic.

**Execution gate**: infrastructure changes land on the **acceptance overlay first**; production waits for a separate go-ahead. This map decides *what* changes; it never applies them to production.

**Skills every session should consult**: `/grilling`, `/domain-modeling`; `/research` for AFK research tickets.

### Verified state as of 2026-08-25 — do not re-litigate

Probed directly against production. **Two of the epic's checklist items are already satisfied**; the scanner reports are partly stale.

| Item | Verified reality |
|---|---|
| SPF | **Already present.** `v=spf1` with Outlook, Scaleway TEM, e-boekhouden and HubSpot includes, terminating in `-all` (hard fail). Moral Fabric's "no SPF record" flag is **wrong**. |
| DMARC | **Already present** at `p=reject; sp=reject`. Mail spoofing of `alkem.io` is closed. |
| Public legal pages | **They exist** — `welcome.alkem.io/legal/` and `/terms`. The apex serves a ~4.5 KB React shell that returns HTTP 200 for *every* path, so a crawler starting at `alkem.io` sees no links and no pages. This is a **discoverability** gap, not a content gap. |
| IPv6 | **Missing everywhere.** No `AAAA` on `alkem.io`; `www` is a CNAME to the apex. **`welcome.` has no v6 either** — its CDN target returns NODATA for `AAAA` and serves v6 only best-effort per PoP. internet.nl scores the category **10/22 today** (nameservers pass, web server fails). |
| DNSSEC | **Unsigned.** No `DS` at the parent. |
| HSTS / CSP / headers | **Absent on `alkem.io`** — no `Strict-Transport-Security`, `Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options` or `Referrer-Policy`. |
| `welcome.alkem.io` headers | **Already hardened** — enforcing CSP with `report-uri` to an existing report-uri.com account, `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. Its only gap is HSTS. Its policy is the starting draft for the app's. |
| CAA | **Absent.** Wildcard `*.alkem.io` from Let's Encrypt. |
| `security.txt` | **Absent** — swallowed by the SPA catch-all at both `/.well-known/security.txt` and `/security.txt`. |

### Decisions taken while charting

- **Acceptance test is the scanner verdict.** Where a control already exists and a scanner still complains, the ticket's job is to make it *discoverable*, not to re-implement it.
- **CSP is measured before it is enforced.** internet.nl only credits the enforcing header, so report-only cannot be the destination — but a blind enforce on an app of unknown origin set breaks production. A report-only measurement window on acceptance produces the policy; enforcing it is then a decided, low-risk change.
- **HSTS ships as `max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`.** Full internet.nl credit without the irreversibility of preload.
- **DNSSEC is gated behind research.** It is not charted as an action until the Scaleway signing support and DS-publication path are known, with a rollback plan. If no managed signing exists, it is ruled out of scope rather than becoming a key-management project.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket -->

- [Research: does Scaleway DNS sign alkem.io, and how does the DS reach the registry?](https://github.com/alkem-io/alkemio/issues/2085) — Signing is technically possible but **gated**: Scaleway signs external domains by API only, publishes **no key-rollover policy** and exposes **no `CDS`/`CDNSKEY`**, so the DS cannot stay in sync automatically; Gandi (the registrar) will not accept a DS at all — it computes one from a submitted KSK. Blast radius of a broken chain is the whole zone at validating resolvers, inbound M365 mail included.
- [Research: how does Moral Fabric detect public legal pages?](https://github.com/alkem-io/alkemio/issues/2088) — The scanner is not a crawler and **does not execute JavaScript**; it coerces any submitted host down to the apex, so pointing it at `welcome.` is impossible. **Server-rendered absolute anchors** from the apex to `welcome.alkem.io` are required *and* sufficient — relative links to the apex's own 200-for-everything host provably fail (`linear.app` is the counterexample). Also surfaced: the apex currently fingerprints as `jurisdiction: unknown`, `usExposed: true`, with **no identifiable owner**.

- [Research: which CAs issue certificates for alkem.io and its subdomains?](https://github.com/alkem-io/alkemio/issues/2086) — Five issuance paths, three live CAs: **Let's Encrypt** (platform wildcard, `welcome.`, `community.`, `dataroom.`), **Certainly** (`blog.` via Ghost/Fastly) and **Sectigo/ZeroSSL**. Microsoft 365 needs no entry — it has never issued for `alkem.io`. Critically, an apex CAA **does not govern `blog.` or `dataroom.` today** (their CNAME targets publish their own RRsets), and **`issuewild` must not be added** — a bare `issue` already covers wildcards, and adding it makes every `issue` ignored for wildcard requests.

- [Research: how does the Scaleway ingress serving alkem.io get IPv6?](https://github.com/alkem-io/alkemio/issues/2087) — **Dual-stack the load balancer, not a CDN.** IPv6 terminates at the LB with no cluster dual-stack needed — and Kapsule could not go dual-stack anyway (single `pod_cidr`/`service_cidr`, unchangeable). The change is additive: LB frontends bind to ports, not IPs. The real risk is **IPv4-only `allowlist-source-range` rules, which 403 every IPv6 client** after real-IP substitution. internet.nl scores the category 10/22 today; an `AAAA` plus a reachable v6 web server on both 80 and 443 takes it to 22/22, **+11 overall**. Also corrected the record: `welcome.` has no IPv6.

## Not yet specified

- **The enforced CSP policy value for `alkem.io`** — cannot be written until the report-only measurement window reports the app's real origin set.
- **The DNSSEC rollout and key-rollover operations plan**, if signing survives its pre-conditions — including the DNSKEY-vs-DS divergence monitor that has to ship *before* any DS goes live.
- **Whether the fingerprint's `jurisdiction` and ownership fields flip** once the legal pages are reachable. If they do, the US-provider observation is being weighed against a known EU entity rather than against nothing — which changes how much of an answer it needs.
- **Whether the other production subdomains sharing the wildcard certificate need the same header set**, once the app's set is agreed.
- **How the closing re-scan evidence is recorded** when the last ticket closes.

## Out of scope

- **HSTS preload-list submission** — effectively irreversible (removal takes months of browser release cycles) and hard-fails any subdomain that is not HTTPS-clean, for zero additional internet.nl score.
- **Writing new legal, terms or imprint content** — Legal/Compliance's call, not engineering's. This map covers only the engineering half of the legal-pages flag.
- **Standing or automated scanner monitoring** — a real idea with its own home in operations; blocking this map on building it would stop it finishing.
- **Header, CSP or IPv6 work on API and internal subdomains** beyond the three hosts in scope.
- **SPF and DMARC work** — verified already satisfied in production; not a gap.
- **`mta-sts.alkem.io` is broken** — the host serves a third-party default certificate that does not match the name, so the TLS handshake fails and **no sender can fetch the policy**, while `_mta-sts` still advertises `v=STSv1`. MTA-STS is therefore advertised but not in force. A real defect, found while inventorying CAs (#2086), but it is mail-transport security and neither scanner tests it. **Filed as a bug on the internal infrastructure tracker** — deliberately not here, since nothing external reports this weakness and a public issue would advertise it.
- **`default-deny-smoke.alkem.io`** — held a Let's Encrypt certificate as recently as 2026-08-13 but resolves NXDOMAIN. Something can still request certificates for that name; worth identifying, but not part of this destination.
t: Wayfinder: Close the internet.nl and Moral Fabric gaps on alkem.io

`alkem.io` returns **no** security headers at all.
