## Description

Alkemio's platform-level authorization grew around a single all-powerful role. `global-admin` gates most administrative actions, so anyone who needs to perform *one* operational task — reset an authorization policy, change a user's email, update an innovation pack — has to be handed the power to do *everything*, permanently. There is no way to give someone exactly the access their job needs, and no way for that access to end.

This Epic covers replacing that model with **purpose-specific platform roles**: a set of narrow, single-responsibility global roles, each owning one family of administrative actions, each independently grantable, auditable, and eventually time-bounded.

Three stories, in the order they land:

| Story | What it does | State |
|---|---|---|
| alkem-io/alkemio#1987 | **Platform Operations Admin** — carves the first action family (authorization reset, operational/maintenance actions) out of `global-admin` into its own role. Proves the pattern on one family. | ✅ Delivered (workspace spec `032`, ADR 0006) |
| #4764 | **Proper design of platform level roles** — the full decomposition: 13 single-purpose global roles across two families (`Platform …`, `Feature …`), per-family privileges replacing the `PLATFORM_ADMIN` catch-all, an assignment rule engine, and an audit trail for every grant and revoke. | 🔨 Slice A code-complete, in review |
| #6319 | **Time-boxed platform roles** — grants that carry an expiry and lapse on their own, so elevated access ends with the work rather than accumulating. | 📋 Ready |

The persona throughout is the **platform operator** — support staff, licensing admins, incident responders — plus the **security owner** who has to answer "who can do what, and who did what" and today cannot.

## Initiative / goal

Reduce standing privilege on the platform. Today, performing any one administrative action requires holding every administrative capability, indefinitely. That is a poor security posture in itself, and it makes the separation-of-duties and least-privilege evidence expected under SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001 impossible to produce — there is nothing to point at except a single role that does everything.

It is also an operational problem, not only a compliance one: it means the set of people who can help with a support ticket is the same set who can delete any space on the platform.

### Hypothesis

Success is that **no routine administrative action requires god mode**, and that access is scoped and time-bounded rather than permanent.

Leading indicators the team can measure:

- **Number of accounts holding `global-admin`** trends to zero (it is a rising count today, because it is the only way to get anything done).
- **Number of administrative surfaces reachable only via `global-admin`** trends to zero — #4764 builds a census of ~76 such surfaces and a build-failing check over it, so this is a number the repo reports rather than an estimate.
- **Every grant and revoke has an audit row** naming the actor, the target and the authorizing role — currently there is no such trail.
- Once #6319 lands, **elevated grants have a median lifetime measured in hours, not "since 2023"**.

## Acceptance criteria and must have scope

**Must have for the Epic to close:**

- [ ] alkem-io/alkemio#1987 — Platform Operations Admin role delivered and in use ✅
- [ ] #4764 **Slice A** (additive) — the 13 roles exist, are grantable, and reach everything their legacy counterparts reach; legacy broad grants still work, so nothing breaks
- [ ] #4764 **Slice B** (subtractive) — legacy broad grants removed; this is the point at which standing privilege actually drops, and it is a hard break shipped as one coordinated release across `server`, `client-web` and `test-suites`
- [ ] #6319 — grants can carry an expiry, and an expired grant stops authorizing

**Sequencing constraints that are not negotiable:**

- Slice B is gated on the **break-glass recovery drill** (FR-013b) passing. Removing the fallback paths before proving the platform can recover from an administrative lockout is how you get an unrecoverable platform.
- #6319 should start **after Slice A, before Slice B**. A lease expiring is a revoke that bypasses the assignment rule engine — including the guard that stops the platform losing its last Platform Roles Admin. The least pleasant moment to discover that is right after the legacy fallback paths are deleted.

**Human gates — these stay human and are not automatable:**

- Security-owner sign-off on the god-mode surface inventory
- Sign-off on each capability withdrawal (some roles lose access they hold today; that is the point, and it needs naming rather than discovering)
- QA acceptance sign-off before the Slice B release
- Acceptance of any residual security risk

## Stakeholders

- **Platform Foundation** — owns delivery of all three stories
- **Security owner** — signs off the god-mode inventory, the capability withdrawals, and any residual risk; the primary beneficiary of the audit trail
- **Support / operations** — the day-to-day holders of the new roles; the withdrawal decisions change what they can do
- **QA** — acceptance sign-off before the Slice B coordinated release
- **Anyone holding `global-admin` today** — needs telling before Slice B, since there is deliberately **no automatic migration** of existing assignments (#4764, FR-012): holders are re-granted by hand, which is a feature, not an oversight

## Timeline

- **alkem-io/alkemio#1987** — done, shipped additively.
- **#4764 Slice A** — code-complete across `server`, `client-web` and `test-suites`; under adversarial review. Currently **not shippable**: the review is at `security-hold` with residual findings open, and several human gates above are unstarted.
- **#4764 Slice B** — blocked on Slice A deploying, positive acceptance sign-off, and the FR-013b break-glass drill.
- **#6319** — ready; starts after Slice A.

**Known blockers / risks:**

- Slice B is a **hard break in one coordinated release** — three repos ship together, with no deprecation window for the removed enum values and mutations. Deprecated aliases were explicitly rejected because they would keep the legacy grant path alive, defeating the purpose.
- The **break-glass drill** is the single gate protecting against permanent administrative lockout, and it has not run.
- Bootstrap seeding of a fresh environment is a live design question: a new deployment must be able to mint its first administrator without that mechanism itself being a god-mode back door.

## Design

Architecture decisions:
- ADR 0006 — Platform Operations Admin role contract (alkem-io/alkemio#1987)
- ADR 0007 — platform role redesign (#4764)

No Figma; this Epic is server-side authorization with a bounded admin-UI slice in `client-web` (offered roles filtered by what the signed-in operator may actually assign, server rejections surfaced as errors — no client-side reimplementation of the assignment rules).
t: Platform roles redesign: replace global admin with purpose-specific roles

b:
Follow-on to #4764 (*Proper design of platform level roles*, workspace spec `027-platform-role-redesign`).

## Description

As a **platform operator**
I want **each operational action to be independently grantable**
So that **someone who needs to re-index search does not also get the ability to rewrite every authorization policy on the platform**

#4764 answers **who** — it decomposes `global-admin` into 13 single-purpose roles. It does not change **what a privilege is**: a privilege still names an *action family*, so one privilege still unlocks every action in it. Platform Operations Admin is the clearest case. It carries one privilege, `PLATFORM_OPERATIONS_ADMIN`, and that privilege gates **13 different mutations** ranging from a geolocation backfill to deleting a Matrix room. Alongside it, `AUTHORIZATION_RESET` gates **8 mutations** in which "reset one user's policy" and "reset every policy on the platform" are the same permission.

The result is god mode at a smaller scale: narrower than `global-admin`, but still all-or-nothing inside its boundary. This story makes the **individual action** the unit of delegation.

There is already precedent in the repo for exactly this split: `LICENSE_RESET` was carved out of the reset family rather than left under `AUTHORIZATION_RESET`. This story finishes the job with a principle rather than case by case.

### The audit trail already knows the actions that authorization cannot see

`PlatformOperationsAuditService.recordOperation()` records a distinct `action` string per mutation. Grepping the source returns **23 named operational actions**:

```
adminCommunicationEnsureAccessToCommunications   adminUpdateGeoLocationData
adminCommunicationMigrateOrphanedConversations   adminUploadFilesFromContentToStorageBucket
adminCommunicationRemoveOrphanedRoom             adminUserAccountDelete
adminCommunicationSyncSpaceHierarchy             aiServerAuthorizationPolicyReset
adminCommunicationUpdateRoomState                aiServerCreateAiPersona
adminIdentityDeleteKratosIdentity                authorizationPlatformRolesAccessReset
adminInAppNotificationsPrune                     authorizationPolicyResetAll
adminMigrateUserAvatar                           authorizationPolicyResetOnPlatform
adminSearchIngestFromScratch                     authorizationPolicyResetToGlobalAdminsAccess
adminUpdateContributorAvatars                    cleanupCollections
deleteUser                                       refreshAllBodiesOfKnowledge
resetLicenseOnAccounts                           updateAssistantActorCapabilities
```

**We can already tell a security owner exactly which of these someone did. We cannot let them do only one of them.** The audit model is finer-grained than the authorization model — the trail distinguishes 23 actions where authorization distinguishes 3 privileges. That asymmetry is the whole story in one line.

## First-pass privilege list

The proposal, against `develop` + #4764 Slice A. Where a privilege is new the existing one it splits out of is named.

### A3 — the reset family (10 surfaces, 2 privileges today)

| Proposed privilege | Surfaces | Why it separates |
|---|---|---|
| `AUTHORIZATION_RESET_ENTITY` | `authorizationPolicyResetOnUser`, `authorizationPolicyResetOnOrganization`, `authorizationPolicyResetOnAccount`, `authorizationPolicyResetToGlobalAdminsAccess` | Single named entity. The routine support action: "this user can't see their space, reset them". Bounded, cheap, recoverable. This is the one that should be handed out. |
| `AUTHORIZATION_RESET_PLATFORM` | `authorizationPolicyResetOnPlatform`, `authorizationPolicyResetAll`, `authorizationPlatformRolesAccessReset`, `aiServerAuthorizationPolicyReset` | Rewrites authorization across the entire platform, asynchronously through the `auth-reset-worker`. `authorizationPolicyResetAll` is plausibly the single highest-blast-radius mutation in the codebase — during #4764's own verification it took down 66 downstream test cells twice, from a stale worker image (`027` residual risk `corr-ts-37`). It is *not* the same permission as fixing one user. |
| `LICENSE_RESET_ACCOUNT` | `licenseResetOnAccount` | One account's entitlements. |
| `LICENSE_RESET_ALL` | `resetLicenseOnAccounts` | Every account on the platform. Same split, same reason. Splits the existing `LICENSE_RESET`. |

### A11 — operational machinery (13 surfaces, 1 privilege today)

All four rows below split out of `PLATFORM_OPERATIONS_ADMIN`.

| Proposed privilege | Surfaces | Why it separates |
|---|---|---|
| `PLATFORM_REINDEX` | `adminSearchIngestFromScratch`, `refreshAllBodiesOfKnowledge`, `cleanupCollections` | Destroy-and-rebuild of derived data. Search is degraded platform-wide until it completes; re-embedding every VC body of knowledge has a real external cost attached to it. Recoverable, but expensive and slow, and typically the thing you *do* want to delegate to whoever is debugging search. |
| `PLATFORM_DATA_MIGRATION` | `adminUpdateContributorAvatars`, `adminUpdateGeoLocationData`, `adminUploadFilesFromContentToStorageBucket`, `adminCommunicationMigrateOrphanedConversations`, `adminMigrateUserAvatar` | Idempotent bulk backfills. Low risk, high volume, run during upgrades. The lowest-privilege row here and a good candidate for a service account. |
| `PLATFORM_MESSAGING_MANAGE` | `adminCommunicationEnsureAccessToCommunications`, `adminCommunicationSyncSpaceHierarchy`, `adminCommunicationUpdateRoomState`, `adminCommunicationRemoveOrphanedRoom` | Matrix housekeeping — a distinct subsystem with its own operators. **Open question below:** `adminCommunicationUpdateRoomState` flips a room to public / world-visible, which is a user-visible privacy change wearing an ops-action costume, and `adminCommunicationRemoveOrphanedRoom` is an irreversible delete. Both may warrant splitting again. |
| `PLATFORM_NOTIFICATION_PRUNE` | `adminInAppNotificationsPrune` | Deletes notification records. Irreversible, unrelated to everything above. |

### Not maintenance at all — reclassify rather than split

| Surfaces | Proposal |
|---|---|
| `updateAssistantActorCapabilities`, `aiServerCreateAiPersona` | These are **configuration** changes to AI behaviour that landed under the operations privilege because that is where the AI-server resolvers happened to sit. They change what the platform does, not repair it. They belong under a settings/configuration privilege — probably `PLATFORM_SETTINGS_ADMIN` — and should move rather than gain a new privilege of their own. |

**Net first pass: `AUTHORIZATION_RESET` and `LICENSE_RESET` become 4; `PLATFORM_OPERATIONS_ADMIN` becomes 4 plus one reclassification.** 3 privileges → 8, covering 23 actions.

### Second pass — the same pattern in #4764's own new privileges

#4764 introduces privileges at family granularity too, so they inherit the same property. Worth re-examining **after Slice A ships**, not before:

- `PLATFORM_USERS_ADMIN` — gates login-email change, Kratos identity deletion, account deletion *and* PII read. Reading a user's PII to answer a support ticket is not the same act as deleting their identity; these are plausibly three privileges.
- `PLATFORM_SUPPORT_ORG_RESOURCES` — gates organization-owned pack/hub updates *and* full template CRUD.
- `PLATFORM_CONTENT_FULL_ACCESS` — already flagged in #4764 as the one role whose blast radius is deliberately not minimised (spec `027`, SC-004's named exception). It is the obvious next target once the pattern is proven.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Should let an operator run `adminSearchIngestFromScratch` while being **denied** `authorizationPolicyResetAll` — the headline case, impossible today
- [ ] Should let an operator reset **one user's** authorization policy while being **denied** the platform-wide reset
- [ ] Should hold every proposed privilege to a stated **splitting rule** (see below) rather than being split by subsystem or by file layout
- [ ] Should keep Platform Operations Admin reaching **everything it reaches today** — the role gains the full new privilege set, so this is additive at role level and no operator loses access
- [ ] Should declare each new privilege in the #4764 census (`a.row.surfaces.ts`) and satisfy the FR-034 reachability derivation, so the drift detector covers the new gates from day one
- [ ] Should make each new privilege independently assertable in the `test-suites` role × A-row matrix (the matrix moves from ~10 reset cells on 2 privileges to per-privilege cells)
- [ ] Should record which privilege authorized each action in the operations audit row, so the trail says *how* the action was authorized and not only *that* it happened
- [ ] Should state, per split, whether Platform Operations Admin remains the sole owner or a second role becomes eligible — a split is only useful if someone can actually be given the narrow half

### The splitting rule this should commit to

Privileges must be the unit of **delegation**, not the unit of implementation, or this ends in 60 privileges nobody can reason about. A split is justified when at least one holds:

1. **A plausible operator wants one and not the other** — a search engineer re-indexing, a support agent resetting one user, an upgrade job backfilling avatars.
2. **Blast radius differs by an order of magnitude** — one entity vs. the whole platform.
3. **Reversibility differs** — an idempotent repair vs. an irreversible delete.

If none of the three holds, the actions stay on one privilege. This rule should live in ADR 0007 (or a successor ADR) so the next person adding an operational mutation has an answer for where to gate it.

## Additional Context

### Why this is not #4764

#4764 splits **who** — 13 roles. This splits **what** — the actions inside a role's boundary. They compose: 13 roles × per-action privileges is the point at which "least privilege" is a statement about actions rather than about job titles. Doing this one first would have been wrong (there was no role to grant the narrow half to); doing it never leaves Operations Admin as a smaller god mode.

### Interaction with #6319 (time-boxed roles)

Per-action privileges and leases solve adjacent halves of the same problem, and together they are noticeably stronger than either alone: a 4-hour grant of `AUTHORIZATION_RESET_PLATFORM` is a defensible break-glass; a permanent grant of it is what we have today. **No hard ordering dependency in either direction** — leases operate on roles, this operates on privileges — but if both land, the natural shape is "narrow privilege, briefly held".

### Cost, stated honestly

- **Enum churn**: `AuthorizationPrivilege` gains ~8 values and, in the subtractive step, loses 3. The GraphQL enum is client-visible, so this is a breaking API change of exactly the kind #4764's Slice B already ships — worth asking whether it should ride that release rather than cut its own.
- **Credential rules multiply**: each new privilege needs its grant in `platform.service.authorization.ts` and its census entry. #4764's Slice A took 11 privileges through that path, so the cost is measured, not guessed.
- **Matrix growth**: the `test-suites` cross-check matrix is a role × surface cross-product; more privileges do not add surfaces, so cell count is roughly unchanged — but per-privilege denial assertions are new.
- **The counter-argument, fairly**: nobody has yet asked to hold "re-index search" without "reset authorization". This is a posture improvement ahead of a demonstrated request. The SOC 2 / ISO 27001 least-privilege evidence named in #6320 is the argument that it is worth doing anyway.

### Scope boundary

**In:** the `AUTHORIZATION_RESET` / `LICENSE_RESET` / `PLATFORM_OPERATIONS_ADMIN` splits above; the reclassification of the two AI-configuration mutations; the splitting rule recorded as an ADR; census, reachability and matrix coverage for each new privilege; recording the authorizing privilege in the operations audit row.

**Out:** splitting #4764's other new privileges (second pass, after Slice A ships); any new role (this changes privileges, not the role set); space- or organization-scoped privileges; leases (#6319).

### Sequencing

Depends on #4764 **Slice A** landing — the census, the reachability derivation and the drift detector are the mechanisms that make a privilege split verifiable rather than hopeful. Best done **before** Slice B if the enum break can ride that release; otherwise after.

## Areas that will be affected

_To be added during refinement_ — first indications: `common/enums/authorization.privilege.ts`, `platform/platform/platform.service.authorization.ts`, `platform/platform-role/verification/` (census + grants + drift), `platform-admin/**` resolvers, `services/ai-server`, `platform-admin/platform-audit-*`, and the `test-suites` role matrix.

**Describe the bug**

Three notification payload builders in `notification.external.adapter.ts` dereference `user.profile.displayName` without a guard. A `User` row whose `profile` is null makes the builder throw a `TypeError`.

On its own that would be a failed request. It is worse than that: `notifyPlatformGlobalRoleChange` in `platform.role.resolver.mutations.ts` invoked its builder **without `await` and without a catch** (both call sites), so the rejection escaped as an unhandled rejection. Under Node's default `--unhandled-rejections=throw`, that **terminates the server process** rather than failing the mutation.

Observed **twice** during live verification of `workspace#027-platform-role-redesign` — once via platform role revocation, once via `createDiscussion` — each time taking the whole server down mid-run.

**To Reproduce**

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Have a `User` row whose `profile` relation is null (an incomplete row — note every caller already loads the user with `relations: { profile: true }`, so this is a data condition, not a missing relation).
2. Trigger any notification whose payload includes that user — e.g. assign or revoke a platform role for them (`assignPlatformRoleToUser` / `removePlatformRoleFromUser`), or have them appear as a recipient of a forum discussion notification.
3. The payload builder throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'displayName')`.
4. The server process exits.

Affected dereference sites:

- `buildPlatformUserRemovedNotificationPayload` — the removed user
- `getUserPayloadOrFail` — the triggering user
- `createUserPayloadFromUser` — each recipient

**Expected behavior**

A notification payload must never be able to take down the process. Two independent expectations:

1. An incomplete user row yields a payload with a usable human identifier via a fallback, rather than throwing.
2. Notification dispatch is best-effort by design, so any downstream failure is contained and logged at ERROR — never propagated as an unhandled rejection.

**Screenshots**

N/A — server-side crash, no UI surface.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

N/A — server-side defect, reproducible independently of client.

**Smartphone (please complete the following information):**

N/A — server-side defect, reproducible independently of client.

**Additional context**

Fixed in #6321.

- `resolveUserDisplayName()` falls back `profile.displayName` → trimmed `firstName lastName` → `email`, so the notification still carries a usable identifier instead of failing to send.
- Dispatch now goes through a `dispatchNotification(promise, eventLabel)` helper matching the existing one in `role.set.resolver.mutations.membership.ts`, so failures are contained and logged in the house structured format (`{ message, event, error }` + stack + `LogContext.NOTIFICATIONS`).
- Regression coverage added in both spec files, verified to fail against the unguarded dereference.

**Areas that will be affected as part of the fix**

- `src/services/adapters/notification-external-adapter/notification.external.adapter.ts`
- `src/platform/platform-role/platform.role.resolver.mutations.ts`

## Summary

Removing a member from a **group conversation** does not revoke their access. There are **two
independent defects**, in different layers. Fixing either one alone leaves removal broken, so both
must land before this issue is closed.

| # | Layer | Defect | Repo | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Matrix room membership | `kick` rejected — `M_FORBIDDEN`, insufficient power level | `matrix-adapter` (+ lib, + room creation) | open |
| 2 | Alkemio authorization | `applyAuthorizationPolicy` never resets, so stale credential rules survive | **`server`** | open |

- [ ] **Cause 1** — Matrix kick succeeds for group-conversation rooms
- [ ] **Cause 2** — conversation authorization policy is reset on re-apply, and re-applied on removal

## Impact

`removeConversationMember` is the only way to revoke access to a group conversation. While either
defect stands, a "removed" member retains **read access** to the room and all future messages.

Discovered during live verification of `workspace#034-messaging-notifications`
(alkem-io/notifications#522), which makes the consequence far more visible — a member you believe
you removed kept receiving message notifications.

**Partially mitigated since:** `sec-server-11` (commit `34ae8047`, on branch `notifications-522`,
PR alkem-io/server#6334) makes removal *authoritative on the Alkemio side* — when the Matrix kick
is rejected it deletes the `conversation_membership` row anyway and logs the divergence. Because
notification recipients are re-read from that table at send time, **notifications now stop
correctly**. That is a notification fix, **not** an access-control fix. Both causes below remain.

---

## Cause 1 — Matrix kick rejected (`matrix-adapter`)

`ConversationService.removeMember` → `CommunicationAdapter.batchRemoveMember` → Go adapter
`KickUser`.

Server log for the batch-remove RPC — note the **top-level** `success: true` beside a **per-room**
failure:

```
communication.room.member.batch.remove-31 - Response payload:
{"success":true,"results":{ ... "success":false,
  "error":{"code":"NOT_ALLOWED",
  "message":"failed to kick user @<uuid>:alkemio.matrix.host from room !<room>:alkemio.matrix.host:
             M_FORBIDDEN (HTTP 403): You cannot kick user @<uuid>:alkemio.matrix.host"}}}
```

`KickUser` calls `getIntentForRoom`, which uses the bot's own intent when the bot is a room member,
otherwise falls back to admin-joining the bot as "PL 100 as room creator". That fallback **assumes
the bot is the room's Matrix creator**. For group-conversation rooms the actual power-level holder
may be a different account, so the admin-join confers no kick rights and Synapse rejects it.
`CreateRoomRequest` has no field for requesting an elevated power level for a specific member at
room-creation time.

Fixing this spans `@alkemio/matrix-adapter-lib`, the Go adapter (id-mapping + Synapse power-level
API) and this repo's room-creation call. Analysis in `server/docs/matrix-admin-reflection.md`
(Finding 1, 2026-07-30).

## Cause 2 — authorization policy is never reset (`server`) — **fixable here**

`src/domain/communication/conversation/conversation.service.authorization.ts:26`

```ts
const conversation = await this.conversationService.getConversationOrFail(conversationID, {
  relations: { authorization: true, room: true },
});
...
conversation.authorization.credentialRules.push(
  this.createCredentialRuleParticipantAccess(participantUserIDs)
);
```

It loads the **persisted** policy — carrying whatever `credentialRules` already exist — and
**pushes** a freshly-computed participant rule on, without first calling
`authorizationPolicyService.reset()`. The convention elsewhere in the codebase is
reset-then-append.

Consequence: rules naming **removed** members are never cleared. They accumulate on every re-apply,
so a removed member keeps `READ` + `CONTRIBUTE` on the conversation and `CREATE_MESSAGE` on its
room — entirely independently of Matrix.

Compounding it: **`ConversationService.removeMember` never calls `applyAuthorizationPolicy` at
all** (verified — the only callers are `message.inbox.service.ts` and `messaging.service.ts`). So
even with `reset()` fixed, the removal path would still not re-apply the policy. **Both parts are
needed:**

1. `reset()` before pushing the participant rule in `applyAuthorizationPolicy` — note this affects
   the add-member callers too and deserves deliberate review;
2. call `applyAuthorizationPolicy` from `removeMember` after the membership row is deleted.

This is **pre-existing** (the code carries `T056`/`T057` markers from the group-conversations work,
not from `034-messaging-notifications`).

## Evidence

Acceptance scenario **US2-AS4** was executed live three times against identical code before the
`sec-server-11` mitigation: **2 of 3 runs failed**, the third passed only after ~18s — an
eventual-consistency window on top of the hard 403. On failing runs the member list still showed
the removed member, and a subsequent message produced a push-queue delta of **2** instead of **1**.

Raw capture `US2-AS4-kick-forbidden-root-cause.log`; screenshots
`US2-AS4-after-remove-confirm.png`, `US2-AS4-after-second-send.png`.

The persisted acceptance spec (`test-suites`, `us2-group-message-notifications.spec.ts`) carries an
explicit scope warning that a green US2-AS4 means "we stopped notifying them", **not** "we revoked
their access" — so it cannot later be cited as proof this issue is resolved.

## Also fixed already (do not re-report)

The `batchRemoveMember` RPC envelope's top-level `success` flag was trusted in isolation
(`response?.success ?? false`), so a rejected per-room kick was silently reported as overall
success — the mutation returned `true` and the dialog closed with no error. Fixed in `d7fe1a3`,
hardened in `36facab`. That made the failure **visible**; it did not make removal work.

## Suggested handling

Cause 2 is contained and can ship independently in `server`; cause 1 wants its own cross-repo spec
("Kick users from rooms"). Until both land, consider whether group-conversation membership should
be presented as revocable in the UI at all.

---

Found by `/forge` during live verification of `workspace#034-messaging-notifications`
(alkem-io/notifications#522). Cause 2 verified by hand against the source.

**Describe the bug**

When Redis becomes unavailable, the whole Node process **exits**. It is not a
degraded-mode or a stream of failed requests — the server dies and does not come
back on its own.

The crash comes from the legacy `redis@3.1.2` client emitting an unhandled
`error` event. That client is **not** the one the OIDC session layer uses (that
one is `ioredis`); it is pulled in by `cache-manager-redis-store`:

```
alkemio-server@0.160.0
├── cache-manager-redis-store 2.0.0
│   └── redis 3.1.2
└── typeorm 0.3.13
    └── redis 3.1.2 (peer)
```

Observed stack:

```
AbortError: Ready check failed: Redis connection lost and command aborted.
It might have been processed.
    at RedisClient.flush_and_error (node_modules/redis/index.js:298:23)
    at RedisClient.connection_gone (node_modules/redis/index.js:603:14)
    at Socket.<anonymous> (node_modules/redis/index.js:231:14)
Emitted 'error' event on RedisClient instance at:
    at RedisClient.on_info_cmd (node_modules/redis/index.js:432:14)
  code: 'UNCERTAIN_STATE',
  command: 'INFO'

Node.js v22.21.1
```

Because nothing handles the `error` event on that client, Node terminates the
process. Both server instances running against the same Redis died
simultaneously, including one started via `pnpm run start:dev` (the watcher
parent exited too, so there was no auto-restart).

**To Reproduce**

1. Start the stack (`pnpm run start:services`) and the server (`pnpm start:dev`).
2. Confirm the API answers, e.g. `GET /api/auth/oidc/id-token-hint` → 401.
3. `docker stop alkemio_dev_redis`
4. Watch the server process exit with the `AbortError` above. Requests to the
   API now fail at the proxy (502); nothing is listening on the GraphQL port.

**Expected behavior**

A Redis outage should be a **degradation**, not a process exit:

- an `error` handler on every Redis client so a connection loss cannot terminate
  the process;
- cache reads/writes fail soft (miss-through to the source of truth) while Redis
  is unavailable;
- the client reconnects on its own once Redis returns, without an operator
  restart.

**Additional context**

Found while manually verifying the OIDC session revocation cascade
(server#6315). That feature explicitly guarantees that `deleteUser` still
succeeds when Redis is down — revocation is best-effort and wrapped in
`try`/`catch`, with unit coverage in `user.service.delete.spec.ts`. That
guarantee **cannot be verified end-to-end on a running platform**, because the
process dies before the mutation can complete. The manual check in
`specs/107-oidc-session-revocation/quickstart.md §6` ("Redis down at deletion →
deletion succeeds") is therefore unrunnable as written until this is fixed.

To be clear about scope: this is **pre-existing and unrelated to #6315's code**.
The OIDC session layer uses `ioredis` and handles its failures; the fatal client
is the cache one.

Impact beyond the blocked test: any Redis blip in an environment where Redis is
not perfectly available takes the API down entirely and needs a manual restart,
turning a cache dependency into a hard availability dependency.

**Areas that will be affected as part of the fix**

- `cache-manager-redis-store` / `redis@3.1.2` wiring (consider migrating this
  client to `ioredis`, which the codebase already depends on, or attaching an
  `error` handler and retry strategy).
- Cache module bootstrap — fail-soft behaviour when the cache is unreachable.
- Possibly a health/readiness signal so an orchestrator sees "degraded" rather
  than a crash loop.
t: BUG: Redis outage crashes the server process (unhandled error event from legacy redis@3.1.2 client)

**Describe the bug**

With Redis unavailable, the API **rejects every request with `401 session_store_unavailable`** — including unauthenticated ones — and each request hangs for roughly **42 seconds** first.

This is the sibling of #6330. That issue fixed the *cache* client (`redis@3.1.2`), which used to kill the process outright; the fix is verified working in #6331. What the live verification of that fix then exposed is that the platform is still fully unavailable during a Redis outage — it now fails **without** crashing instead of failing **by** crashing. The remaining fault is in the **OIDC session layer**, which uses `ioredis`, and is entirely pre-existing on `develop`.

Three independent defects combine to produce it:

**1. Every request performs a Redis session lookup — even anonymous ones**

`src/core/auth/oidc/strategies/cookie-session.strategy.ts:64` resolves the session id from `req.sessionID`:

```ts
const sid =
  typeof req.sessionID === 'string' && req.sessionID.length > 0
    ? req.sessionID
    : req.cookies?.[this.sessionCookieName];
if (typeof sid !== 'string' || sid.length === 0) return null;

let payload: AlkemioSessionPayload | null;
try {
  payload = await this.sessionStore.get(sid);
} catch (err) {
  throw new SessionStoreUnavailableError(err);
}
```

`express-session` assigns `req.sessionID` on **every** request — a freshly generated random id when no session cookie was sent (`saveUninitialized: false` controls only whether it is *persisted*, not whether it is *generated*). The strategy therefore cannot distinguish a real session id from one express-session invented microseconds earlier, and issues a `sessionStore.get(sid)` for a key that cannot exist.

While Redis is healthy this is invisible — a wasted GET returning null, then correctly degrading to anonymous. While Redis is down it throws, and an anonymous request that needs no session at all fails. Observed directly: `{ platform { id } }` sent with **no cookies** returned `200` before the outage, `401` during it, `200` after.

**2. The session `ioredis` clients are constructed with no options**

| Client | Site | Options |
|---|---|---|
| express-session store | `src/main.server.ts:105` | `new Redis({ host, port })` |
| `SESSION_STORE_HANDLE` | `src/core/auth/oidc/oidc.module.ts:56` | `new Redis({ host, port })` |
| health probe | `src/core/health/health.module.ts:37` | `lazyConnect`, `maxRetriesPerRequest: 1`, `connectTimeout: 500`, `enableOfflineQueue: false` |

The two session clients get ioredis defaults: `enableOfflineQueue: true`, so commands issued while disconnected are **queued rather than rejected**, and `maxRetriesPerRequest: 20` with backoff `min(times × 50, 2000) ms`, so a queued command burns roughly **10.5 seconds** before failing. Several session operations per request, in series, accounts for the ~42 s measured.

Note that the health client in the same repo already sets exactly the four options that would turn this into an instant failure, with a comment explaining why. The knowledge is present; it was applied to the probe surface and not to the two clients every request depends on.

**3. `SessionStoreUnavailableError` never reaches its own exception filter on the GraphQL path**

`src/core/auth/oidc/strategies/cookie-session.exception-filter.ts` exists specifically to answer this condition correctly — **503 with `Retry-After: 5`, re-setting the session cookie rather than clearing it** (FR-022b). It is `@Catch(SessionStoreUnavailableError)` and reads `host.switchToHttp()`.

But `src/core/interceptors/auth.interceptor.ts:205` preserves only two error types through its passport callback:

```ts
if (
  err instanceof BearerValidationError ||
  err instanceof CookieSessionInvalidError
) {
  reject(err);
  return;
}
reject(new AuthenticationException(...));   // ← SessionStoreUnavailableError lands here
```

`SessionStoreUnavailableError` is absent from that allow-list, so on the GraphQL path it is wrapped into `AuthenticationException` and surfaces as **401 `UNAUTHENTICATED`, numericCode 11101** instead of 503. Confirmed in the logs: `ERROR [auth] session_store_unavailable - AuthenticationException … at auth.interceptor.ts:213`.

The consequence is not cosmetic. A SPA reads 401 as *"your session is invalid, log in again"*, whereas 503 + `Retry-After` means *"come back in five seconds"*. As written, any Redis blip is liable to present to users as a forced logout / redirect loop rather than a transient outage.

**To Reproduce**

1. Start the dev stack and the server (any branch — this is pre-existing on `develop`).
2. Confirm an unauthenticated query answers: `curl -s -X POST localhost:4000/graphql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":"{ platform { id } }"}'` → `200`.
3. `docker stop alkemio_dev_redis`
4. Repeat the same **cookie-less** query. Observed: it hangs ~42 s, then returns `401` with `{"errors":[{"message":"session_store_unavailable","extensions":{"code":"UNAUTHENTICATED","numericCode":11101}}]}`.
5. `docker start alkemio_dev_redis` → returns to `200` in ~3 ms.

Note that `:6379` on the dev stack is a Traefik-published route to the same `alkemio_dev_redis` container, so stopping that container is a total outage rather than a partial one.

**Expected behavior**

- A request that carries **no session cookie** must not touch the session store at all, and must resolve to anonymous regardless of Redis health.
- A request that **does** carry a session must fail **fast** — sub-second — when the store is unreachable, not queue behind ~20 reconnect attempts.
- Store-unreachable must surface as **503 + `Retry-After`** on every transport including GraphQL, with the session cookie preserved, so clients retry instead of treating it as an authentication failure and logging the user out.
- Overall: a Redis outage should degrade the platform, not make it reject all traffic.

**Additional context**

Found while running the live outage verification for #6330 / PR #6331 on 2026-08-03. Evidence from that run (server PID 2963681, outage window 3 m 23 s):

- the cache layer behaved exactly as designed — process survived on one PID, exactly two `[cache]` log records (one per transition, no retry flood), automatic recovery with `200` in 3.5 ms and no restart;
- and yet every request during the window still returned `401 session_store_unavailable`.

The quickstart results table on that PR records this as **SC-009 FAILED** rather than rewording the criterion, and the finding is written up at https://github.com/alkem-io/server/pull/6331#issuecomment-5168134848.

Related root-cause note: #6330 was *one unsafe cache bootstrap copy-pasted into two modules*; this is *one safe Redis bootstrap that was not propagated to the two clients that mattered*. Same underlying cause — per-site Redis client construction with no shared factory — pointing in opposite directions. PR #6331 introduced `src/core/cache/cache.store.factory.ts` as the single construction point for the cache client; the same treatment for the `ioredis` clients would close this class of bug rather than this instance of it.

**Areas that will be affected as part of the fix**

- `src/core/auth/oidc/strategies/cookie-session.strategy.ts` — distinguish a cookie-borne session id from an express-session-generated one; skip the store lookup entirely when the request carries no session cookie.
- `src/main.server.ts:105` and `src/core/auth/oidc/oidc.module.ts:56` — ioredis client options (`enableOfflineQueue`, `maxRetriesPerRequest`, `connectTimeout`, `commandTimeout`), ideally via one shared factory mirroring `src/core/health/health.module.ts` and the cache factory added in #6331.
- `src/core/interceptors/auth.interceptor.ts:205` — add `SessionStoreUnavailableError` to the preserved-error allow-list so the 503 filter is reachable from the GraphQL path.
- Regression coverage: an anonymous request must not call the session store; a store-unreachable failure must be fast and must surface as 503, not 401.
t: BUG: Redis outage makes the API reject every request (~42s hang, 401 session_store_unavailable) — untuned session ioredis clients + anonymous requests hitting the store

**Describe the bug**

Renaming a state (phase) on an Innovation Flow does not persist the new name to the Callouts sitting on that phase. Their `flow-state` classification tagset keeps the **old** name in the database, which is no longer one of the template's `allowedValues` — so every Callout on the renamed phase stops matching any phase filter and disappears from all tabs.

The cause is a missing save in `TagsetService.updateTagsetsSelectedValue` (`src/domain/common/tagset/tagset.service.ts:226`). The rename branch mutates the entity and `continue`s without persisting, while the branch immediately below it — the fallback-to-default branch — does save:

```ts
if (valueRenamed && tagsetSelectedValue === valueRenamed.old) {
  tagset.tags = [valueRenamed.new];
  continue;                                    // <-- never saved
}
tagset.tags = [newDefaultValue];
await this.tagsetRepository.save(tagset);      // <-- saved
```

The trailing `await this.save(innovationFlow)` in the caller cannot rescue it: `InnovationFlow → TagsetTemplate` is `cascade: false`, and `TagsetTemplate → tagsets` is `cascade: false`, so the in-memory mutation is never flushed.

**To Reproduce**

1. Open a Space with an Innovation Flow and at least one Callout on a phase — e.g. `Explore`.
2. Confirm the Callout is visible under the `Explore` tab.
3. Edit the Innovation Flow and rename the state `Explore` → `Discover`.
4. Return to the Space. The `Discover` tab is empty, and the Callout appears under no tab at all.
5. In the database, `tagset.tags` for that Callout still reads `Explore`, while the template's `allowedValues` now contains `Discover`.

**Expected behavior**

Renaming a phase should carry every Callout on that phase to the new name. After the rename the Callout stays visible, under the renamed tab.

**Additional context**

Found during the `xhigh` code review of #6339 (story #6021) and verified by reading the code path; it was deliberately left out of that PR because it lives in an untouched file with a different blast radius.

This is a strong candidate for the "I thought this was fixed" note on the alkem-io/alkemio#1846 whiteboard: it produces the **same** user-visible symptom as #6021 and #4970 — a Callout that silently vanishes from every tab — but through phase *editing* rather than cross-space transfer. Fixing the transfer path alone would not make this go away.

Related: alkem-io/server#6021, alkem-io/server#4970, alkem-io/client-web#9353, PR alkem-io/server#6339.

There is also an adjacent, separate defect worth scoping alongside this one: `createStateOnInnovationFlow` and `deleteStateOnInnovationFlow` (`src/domain/collaboration/innovation-flow/innovation.flow.service.ts:459` / `:501`) never refresh `innovationFlow.flowStatesTagsetTemplate`, so adding or deleting a phase leaves `allowedValues` drifting from the flow's actual states.

**Areas that will be affected as part of the fix**

- `src/domain/common/tagset/tagset.service.ts` — `updateTagsetsSelectedValue`, one added `await this.tagsetRepository.save(tagset);` before the `continue`.
- `src/domain/common/tagset/tagset.service.spec.ts` — regression test asserting the rename branch persists (the existing suite does not cover it).

Suggested fix:

```diff
 if (valueRenamed && tagsetSelectedValue === valueRenamed.old) {
   tagset.tags = [valueRenamed.new];
+  await this.tagsetRepository.save(tagset);
   continue;
 }
```
t: BUG: renaming an innovation-flow state does not persist to callout tagsets

## Description

Slice A of the platform role redesign (#4764) adds 13 purpose-specific roles without taking
anything away. Slice B (#6345) deletes `global-admin` and the nine other legacy global roles
outright.

Between those two events, **every human who holds a legacy role has to be moved onto the new ones
by hand.** There is deliberately **no automatic migration** — FR-012 makes that a design decision,
not an oversight: a script that maps `global-admin` onto a bundle of new roles would recreate the
god-mode grant it is the point of this work to remove, and it would do so without anyone deciding
that a given person still needs that access.

This issue owns that migration. **It is done entirely from the admin console — no database access,
no GraphQL, no engineer required for the normal path.** Everything below is written so a product
support person can execute it. The three places where the console genuinely cannot help are named
explicitly in §7, along with who to hand them to.

## Who does this, and what access they need

| Step | Who | What they must hold |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Capture the legacy holders (before deploy) | Support | An account that still holds **Global Admin** (or Global Support). The legacy panel is shown only to a legacy-admin-equivalent account — a Platform Roles Admin **cannot** see it |
| 2. Decide the mapping | Support + role owner | — |
| 3. Notify holders | Support | — |
| 4. Deploy + authorization reset | Engineering | — |
| 5. Re-grant (after deploy) | **Two** people, both **Platform Roles Admin** | Nobody can grant a role to themselves, so this is inherently a two-person job |
| 6. Verify | Support | Platform Roles Admin (to read holder lists) |

The whole job happens on one page: **Admin → Authorization → Roles**
(`/admin/authorization/roles`). It has two parts — a **role picker** with the 13 new roles and
their current members, and, below it, a section headed **"Legacy roles (revoke only)"**.

---

## 1. Capture the legacy holders — before anything is removed

This replaces the old SQL export (server task **T071a**). It is the **only** artifact that survives
the cleanup: the cleanup migration writes **no audit records at all** (FR-018's single documented
carve-out — the migration is considered its own record), so once Slice B deploys, the record of who
held what is gone.

**Run this on the target environment on deploy day, immediately before the deploy — not at
PR-open.** Holders change.

1. Sign in with an account that still holds **Global Admin**.
2. Go to **Admin → Authorization → Roles**.
3. Scroll to **"Legacy roles (revoke only)"**. Each legacy role that has at least one holder is
   listed with its holders as `Display Name (email)`.
4. Copy every name + email into the tracking sheet (template in §3), one row per person per role.
   Somebody holding three legacy roles gets three rows.
5. Screenshot the whole section and attach it to the Slice B PR alongside the sheet.

**Read the empty states carefully — they are not the same thing:**

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| A role is **not listed at all** | That role has zero holders | Nothing. Record "0 holders" for it |
| *"No one currently holds a legacy role."* | Genuinely nobody holds any of the ten | Record it and move on |
| *"Unable to load the current holders of this role."* | The read **failed or was refused** | **Do not record this as empty.** Sign out, sign back in with a Global Admin account, retry. If it persists, stop and escalate — deploying past this loses the list |

**What the panel covers.** All ten legacy roles: Global Admin, Global Support, Global License
Manager, Global Community Reader, Global Spaces Reader, Global Platform Manager, Global Support
Manager, Platform Beta Tester, Platform VC Campaign, AI Assistant Access. Legacy roles can only be
held by **people**, never by organizations (their organization policy is 0/0), so the user list is
complete — there is no second list to go and find.

**The panel disappears at Slice B.** It exists only for this window.

---

## 2. Decide the mapping, one person at a time

The audit in #4764 gives the intended successor for each legacy role. It is a **decision per
person**, not a lookup — the whole point is that someone confirms each holder still needs the
access.

| Legacy role | Intended successor | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Global Admin | Platform Roles Admin + whichever families the person actually performs | The one that must not be mapped mechanically |
| Global Support | Platform Operations Admin and/or Platform Users Admin and/or Platform Support | Three distinct families bundled together today |
| Global License Manager | Platform License Manager | Loses the `PLATFORM_ADMIN` catch-all it also carried |
| Global Platform Manager | Platform Settings Admin | |
| Global Spaces Reader | Platform Spaces Reader | Service accounts only; re-seeds automatically — see §7 |
| Global Community Reader | *(none)* | Removed — broad PII read judged redundant |
| Global Support Manager | *(none)* | Removed — near-inert, gates no top-level action |
| Platform Beta Tester | Feature Beta Tester **and/or** Feature Organization Creator | See §2a |
| AI Assistant Access | Feature Virtual Assistant | |
| Platform VC Campaign | **undecided — see §2b** | |

**"No longer needs access" is a valid and expected outcome.** Record it as the decision; leaving a
row blank is not the same thing.

**Mapping Global Admin mechanically would defeat the entire feature.** If everyone who held it is
handed all thirteen new roles, standing privilege has not dropped — it has been renamed.

### 2a. Beta Tester splits in two

Platform Beta Tester carries organization creation *and* a beta/trial entitlement today.

- **The entitlement is safe with no action.** Granting the role wrote an independent
  `ACCOUNT_LICENSE_PLUS` credential onto the person's *account*, and the cleanup only deletes rows
  of the retired role types — so it survives untouched.
- **What is genuinely lost is the ability to create organizations.** Any beta tester who creates
  organizations needs **Feature Organization Creator** granted explicitly.

So for every beta tester, the question to answer is: *does this person create organizations?* Ask
them — the console cannot tell you.

### 2b. VC Campaign has no successor, and it is not inert

The audit recorded it as *"no enforced platform grant found → Removed"*, which is true server-side
and wrong overall: the **client gates the dashboard campaign banner on it**. The role is the
*targeting* half of a two-axis gate — the entitlement says who is *allowed* a Virtual Contributor,
the role says who gets *shown the offer*.

Removing it without a replacement permanently loses the ability to promote VC creation to a chosen
subset, along with the record of who was targeted. The VC creation flow itself survives in user and
organization account settings, both entitlement-gated.

**A product decision is needed before the role is deleted** — it cannot be retrofitted afterwards.
The current targeting list is exactly what the Platform VC Campaign group in step 1 shows; capture
it even if the decision is "drop it".

---

## 3. Tracking sheet

One row per person per legacy role. This sheet is the migration's only record — treat it as the
deliverable.

```
Name | Email | Legacy role(s) held | Decision (new role(s) / none) | Decided by | Notified (date) | Re-granted (date) | Re-granted by | Confirmed by holder
```

---

## 4. Notify everyone on the list, before the deploy

There is no automatic migration and no in-platform announcement for this — send the mail yourself.
Everyone on the sheet must know that **their platform access stops at the release**, and either
what they will get back or that they will not.

---

## 5. The re-grant window, after the deploy

Engineering deploys Slice B and runs the authorization reset (server task **T088**). Then support
re-grants by hand from the sheet. **Service accounts re-seed themselves automatically; humans do
not.**

Between the deploy and the re-grants, **no human holds a platform role.** That is a genuine outage
of administrative capability, not a formality — keep the window short and scheduled.

**To grant a role:** Admin → Authorization → Roles → pick the role → **Add members** → search by
name or email → **Add**. To revoke: **Remove** next to the person, then confirm.

**Five rules will refuse you, and each names itself at the end of the rejection message.** These
are not bugs:

| Rejection says | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `self-assignment` | Nobody can grant *or revoke* a platform role on their own account | The other Platform Roles Admin does it. This is why the window needs two people |
| `last-roles-admin` | The final Platform Roles Admin cannot be revoked | Grant the replacement first. The practical floor is **two holders** |
| `holder-kind` | A `Platform …` role was aimed at an organization | Only the three `Feature …` roles can be held by an organization |
| `audit-reader-exclusion` | Platform Audit Reader cannot be combined with any other `Platform …` role | Pick one; the Audit Reader watches the others |
| `spaces-reader-service-account` | Platform Spaces Reader was aimed at a normal account | See §7 — hand to engineering, and check the person actually needs it |

**Finish the window with at least two Platform Roles Admin holders.** One is a lockout waiting to
happen.

---

## 6. Verify

1. **Legacy section is gone.** The "Legacy roles (revoke only)" section no longer renders — the
   roles behind it no longer exist.
2. **Every sheet row is closed.** Each row has either a re-grant date or an explicit
   "no longer needs access".
3. **Spot-check from the role side.** For each new role, open it and use **Filter members…** with
   the person's email to confirm they are in it. (There is no per-user role view in the console —
   check from the role, not the user.)
4. **Two Platform Roles Admin holders exist.**
5. **Ask.** Mail everyone who was re-granted and confirm they can do their job. A role that looks
   right in the console and does not work in practice is the failure mode this step catches; record
   the answer in the last column.

---

## 7. The three things the console cannot do

Honest limits, so nobody discovers them mid-window:

1. **Marking an account as a service account** (required before Platform Spaces Reader can be
   granted) has no console affordance. **You almost certainly do not need it**: the service
   accounts that hold this role are re-seeded automatically on deploy. If a real person needs it,
   hand it to engineering — and question the request first.
2. **Two "ghost" legacy credentials** exist in the database under slightly different spellings than
   the code expects (`global-spaces-reader` / `global-community-reader`). They are **invisible in
   the console and grant nothing** — a known dormant defect, not a hidden privilege. Nothing to
   migrate; the cleanup deletes them. Do not go looking for them.
3. **The cleanup writes no audit record.** By design (FR-018). Your sheet is the record. This is
   why step 1 cannot be skipped or done from memory.

---

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Legacy holder list captured from the admin console on the target environment **immediately
      before** the Slice B deploy — sheet + screenshot attached to the Slice B PR and handed to the
      deploy runbook
- [ ] No group in that capture was recorded as empty on the strength of an *"Unable to load…"*
      message
- [ ] A per-holder decision recorded for every person in the capture — including
      "no longer needs access"
- [ ] Every beta tester asked whether they create organizations; those who do are granted **Feature
      Organization Creator**
- [ ] A decision recorded for VC campaign targeting **before** the role is removed, with the
      current target list captured either way
- [ ] Everyone on the list notified before the deploy — no automatic migration, access stops at the
      release
- [ ] Re-grant window executed after the deploy; **at least two** Platform Roles Admin holders exist
      at the end of it
- [ ] Post-window check: legacy section gone, every sheet row closed, and every re-granted operator
      has confirmed they can do their job

## Risks

- **The capture is a single manual step whose omission is silent.** Nothing fails if it is skipped;
  the information simply ceases to exist once the cleanup runs.
- **An *"Unable to load…"* message read as "nobody holds this"** loses a whole role's audience just
  as completely as skipping the step.
- **The window is a real outage of administrative capability**, not a formality.
- **Mapping Global Admin mechanically renames god mode instead of removing it.**

## Appendix — fallback if the console panel is unavailable

Only if the legacy section cannot be reached at all (and only with engineering): the same data is
`platform.roleSet.usersInRole(role: …)` per legacy role over GraphQL, and, last resort, a
`credential` join in the database over the twelve retired credential types. Both produce the same
list the console shows; neither is the intended path.

## Related

- Epic #6320
- #4764 — Slice A (additive), where the new roles are introduced
- #6345 — Slice B (subtractive), which removes the legacy roles and triggers this migration
t: Platform roles: migrate existing legacy-role holders onto the new roles

## Description

**Slice B is the half of the platform role redesign where standing privilege actually drops.**

Slice A (#4764) adds the 13 purpose-specific roles alongside everything that exists today. Every authorization rule is a union — `{new owning role} ∪ legacy` — so nothing is taken away and nothing breaks. That is deliberate, and it is also why Slice A on its own improves nothing measurable: `global-admin` still reaches every surface.

Slice B removes the other half of every one of those unions. After it ships, an administrative action is reachable **only** by the role that owns it.

It is **breaking, has no deprecation window, and ships as one coordinated release** across `server`, `client-web` and `test-suites`. Deprecated aliases were explicitly rejected: a working legacy enum value keeps the legacy grant path alive, which is the thing being removed.

## What changes

**The god-mode mechanism itself**
- The root policy's blanket CRUD+GRANT to `global-admin` over every entity tree is deleted; `createRootCredentialRules()` becomes `[READ, PLATFORM_CONTENT_FULL_ACCESS] → platform-content-full-access` and `GRANT` leaves the root entirely
- The `GLOBAL_SUPPORT` platform-subtree cascade is deleted — Support's reach becomes A6/A7/A15 only
- `PLATFORM_ADMIN` is removed from the privilege enum, along with its **57 call sites across 33 files**

**The vocabulary** (all breaking, no aliases)
- 10 `RoleName` values removed, and the 10 matching `AuthorizationCredential` values
- `GRANT_GLOBAL_ADMINS` → renamed **`PLATFORM_ROLES_ASSIGN`**
- Legacy credentials dropped from **every** remaining grant set, so each privilege is held by its owning role alone

**Surface removals**
- The 4 generic credential mutations (`grant`/`revokeCredentialTo(User|Organization)`) — service methods retained, bootstrap needs them
- The Wingback integration — 3 directories, 3 admin mutations, references across 42 files
- `updateUserPlatformSettings` and `updateOrganizationPlatformSettings`; `updateSpacePlatformSettings` → `adminUpdateSpaceVisibility` (visibility only)
- New: `updateActorNameID`, gated on `UPDATE_NAMEID` — renaming becomes an owner-level protected update rather than a platform-admin one

**Data**
- Forward-only migration deleting `credential` rows of every retired type, then the `role` rows on the platform role-set
- **It writes no audit records** — FR-018's single carve-out; the migration is the record. This is why the export in #6344 must run first

## Progress

Work has started on branch `feat/027-platform-role-redesign-slice-b` in all three repos (uncommitted at time of writing).

**6 of 31 Slice B tasks complete.**

| Repo | Done | Files touched |
|---|---|---|
| `server` | 6 / 18 | 185 (114 modified, 41 deleted, 4 added, 26 partially staged) |
| `client-web` | 0 / 4 | 26 |
| `test-suites` | 0 / 9 | 151 |

**Done:** T072 (root god-mode rule deleted) · T073 (`GLOBAL_SUPPORT` cascade deleted) · T075 (`GRANT_GLOBAL_ADMINS` → `PLATFORM_ROLES_ASSIGN`) · T078 (platform-settings mutations) · T079 (Wingback) · T080 (credential mutations)

**Remaining in `server`:** T071 · T071a · T074 (`PLATFORM_ADMIN`, 57 sites) · T076 (legacy credentials out of every grant set) · T077 (enum values) · T081 (seed migration) · T082 (cleanup DML) · T083 (schema regen + breaking approval) · T083a (verification artifacts re-closed against the Slice B surface)

`client-web` (4) and `test-suites` (9) have not started.

## Hard prerequisites — not startable without these

- [ ] **Slice A deployed** and positive acceptance sign-off obtained
- [ ] **T071 — the break-glass recovery drill has run, with evidence attached.** This is the only gate protecting against permanent administrative lockout, and it has never been executed. Slice B deletes the fallback paths; running the drill afterwards is not a test, it is an incident.
- [ ] **T071a — the operator re-grant list exported** from the target environment, immediately before deploy (#6344)
- [ ] CODEOWNER `BREAKING-APPROVED` on the schema diff, with `change-report.json` matching the declared breaking set exactly and nothing more

## Areas affected

**`server`** — the authorization root policy; the platform, space, community, collaboration and licensing authorization services; `platform-admin` mutations; the platform-role resolver and rule engine; the privilege, role-name and credential enums; the seed migration plus a new cleanup migration; the GraphQL schema contract. Largest single cluster is `src/services/external` (28 files — Wingback removal).

**`client-web`** — regenerated codegen (10 `RoleName` + 10 `AuthorizationCredential` values disappear, `PLATFORM_ADMIN` goes, `GRANT_GLOBAL_ADMINS` renames); removal of the legacy-roles panel; the admin role pages; and **every remaining reference to a retired identifier — the build breaks the instant the server drops the values**.

> ⚠️ The sweep that was supposed to enumerate those references (`client-web` T011, marked done) produced no recorded list. At least two functional sites are known and are **not** cosmetic: `DashboardWithMemberships.tsx` and `DashboardWithoutMemberships.tsx` gate the VC campaign banner on `PLATFORM_VC_CAMPAIGN`. Deleting the role there is a product decision, not a build fix — see #6344.

**`test-suites`** — the full denial matrix turns on. Today **all 134 executable matrix cells are ALLOW and zero DENY cells run**, because `it.skipIf(!isStageB())` gates them: while `global-admin` still reaches every surface a denial would be meaningless. Slice B is where the suite starts proving separation of duties rather than capability. Also: the four legacy `TestUser` fixtures are removed (T021).

**Operations** — a planned re-grant window after deploy in which **no human holds a platform role** until the break-glass Roles Admin re-grants by hand (#6344). Service accounts re-seed automatically.

**`kratos-webhooks` / `oidc-service`** — identity lifecycle touched by some admin actions; coupling to be confirmed.

## Risks

- **One coordinated release across three repos, no deprecation window.** A client built against the removed enum values breaks the instant the server drops them.
- **The break-glass drill has never run.** It is the single control standing between this release and an unrecoverable platform.
- **The cleanup migration is not reversible and leaves no trail.** Forward-only DML, no audit records by design.
- **Several roles lose access they hold today.** That is the point of the feature, but each withdrawal needs naming and signing off rather than discovering — in particular Platform Content Full Access is narrowed to read plus its own enumerated surface, dropping blanket create/update/delete.

## Related

- Epic #6320
- #4764 — Slice A (additive), the prerequisite
- #6344 — migrating existing holders onto the new roles
- #6319 — time-boxed roles; should land **after** Slice A and **before** Slice B (an expiring lease is a revoke that bypasses the rule engine, including the last-Roles-Admin guard)

## Summary

Opening a Collabora document (and other Collabora document-attribution paths) makes the user wait **~8 seconds** in production. The editor URL itself resolves in ~47 ms — the wait is a best-effort analytics record the user never asked for, `await`ed **inline before the response returns**.

## Impact

- `collaboraEditorUrl` (document open) — the primary user-facing ~8 s stall.
- `replaceCollaboraDocument`, `importCollaboraDocument` — same penalty on those mutations.
- The `reportOfficeDocumentWindow` background RabbitMQ consumer pays the same query on every contribution event.

Production APM (`CollaboraEditorUrl` transaction) is flat below one second until the rollout on **26 June 2026 ~12:00**, then steps straight to 5–8 s. Filtered to `> 5,000,000 µs` the series *begins* on 26 June — zero such transactions existed in the 46 days prior. A control transaction on the same page is flat across the boundary, ruling out a platform-wide deploy effect.

## Root cause

#6187 added a `COLLABORA_DOCUMENT_OPENED` analytics record (and sibling `_REPLACED` / `_UPLOADED` records) to the resolver, `await`ed before the response returns. Attributing each record to a space calls `getCommunityForCollaboraDocumentOrFail` — a TypeORM `findOne(Space)` whose `where` ORs two five-level relation paths:

```
space -> collaboration -> calloutsSet -> callouts -> contributions -> collaboraDocument
space -> collaboration -> calloutsSet -> callouts -> framing       -> collaboraDocument
```

TypeORM expands each into a full relation tree, joins the entire callout graph, and filters only at the leaf. That single `SELECT` measured **7,917 ms** in trace `c4a6bf41dcec6ceba4aa3bb5c94889d4` (2026-07-25, `alkemio-server` 0.159.0). By contrast the neighbouring `getLevelZeroSpaceIdForCommunity` query runs in 9.8 ms against the same DB at the same moment — the database is fine, the query *shape* is not.

Two independent defects:
- **D1** — analytics blocks the response (should be detached / best-effort, off the hot path).
- **D2** — the space lookup behind it costs ~8 s (should be a leaf-first unique-index seek, reusing `getLevelZeroSpaceIdForCalloutsSet`).

## Temporary fix (this issue) — PR #6354, base `release/71`

To remove the user penalty now, PR #6354 **comments out** (does not delete) the four best-effort analytics blocks that trigger the ~8 s `getCommunityForCollaboraDocumentOrFail` lookup:

1. `collabora.document.resolver.queries.ts` — `collaboraEditorUrl` / `COLLABORA_DOCUMENT_OPENED`
2. `collabora.document.resolver.mutations.ts` — `replaceCollaboraDocument` / `COLLABORA_DOCUMENT_REPLACED`
3. `callout.resolver.mutations.ts` — `importCollaboraDocument` / `COLLABORA_DOCUMENT_UPLOADED`
4. `collaborative-document-integration.service.ts` — `reportOfficeDocumentWindow` background consumer

**Trade-off:** these analytics records (`COLLABORA_DOCUMENT_OPENED` / `_REPLACED` / `_UPLOADED`) are temporarily suppressed. All user-facing behavior is unchanged; the expensive method is left intact (its removal belongs to the proper fix). The corresponding unit-test assertions are skipped with pointers to the follow-up.

## Proper fix (follow-up) — spec PR #6350

Feature `110-collabora-editor-url-latency` addresses both defects properly: detach the three user-facing analytics paths (D1) and replace `getCommunityForCollaboraDocumentOrFail` with a leaf-first lookup reusing `getLevelZeroSpaceIdForCalloutsSet`, deleting the old method (D2). When that lands, the four commented blocks and the skipped tests must be restored/replaced.

## Verification

- **Pre-merge:** gates green (tsc + biome, nest build, full Vitest suite).
- **Post-deploy:** the `CollaboraEditorUrl` APM transaction returns to its pre-26-June band (below 1 s); the `> 5,000,000 µs` filter yields nothing under normal operation. Control transaction `CalloutsOnCalloutsSetUsingClassification` should remain flat.

## Links

- Temporary fix PR: #6354 (base `release/71`)
- Proper fix spec PR: #6350 (feature `110-collabora-editor-url-latency`)
- Regression introduced by: #6187
- Original report: alkem-io/wopi-service#29
t: Collabora document open blocks ~8s on inline analytics attribution (getCommunityForCollaboraDocumentOrFail)

## Summary

Proper fix for the ~8 s Collabora document-open stall reported in #6356. That issue shipped a **temporary mitigation** in **Release 71** (PR #6354, base `release/71`) which simply *commented out* the four best-effort analytics blocks. This ticket tracks the **proper implementation** — feature `110-collabora-editor-url-latency`, merged in **PR #6350** — to be **released with the next release**.

The proper fix **fully supersedes** the Release 71 quick fix: it restores/preserves all Collabora analytics through the intended paths, with **no temporary early return, no commented-out analytics body, and no disabled analytics suite** left behind.

## Root cause (recap)

Two independent defects behind the stall (full detail in #6356):

- **D1** — best-effort analytics were `await`ed inline on the user-facing path, so the caller waited for work it never requested.
- **D2** — the space-ownership lookup (`getCommunityForCollaboraDocumentOrFail`) started from the broad `Space` aggregate root, OR-ing two five-level relation paths through the callout graph and filtering only at the leaf — a single `SELECT` measured at **7,917 ms** in production.

## What PR #6350 changes

### D1 — detach analytics from user-facing paths (sites 1–3)

Open, replace, and upload now synchronously publish distinct typed lifecycle events through the existing global `EventEmitter2`:

- `collabora.document.opened`
- `collabora.document.replaced`
- `collabora.document.uploaded`

- Publication uses `emit` (not `emitAsync`) and returns `void` — a slow or never-settling subscriber cannot delay the GraphQL response.
- A singleton subscriber owns attribution lookup, reporter dispatch, timing, and failure containment.
- The event boundary retains only a fresh, frozen attribution snapshot: `{ actorID, isAnonymous, guestName }` — no request-scoped `ActorContext`, credentials, session timestamps, or delegation metadata.
- Publication happens strictly **after** the primary work completes (open: after the editor URL resolves; replace: after the file swap + optional rename; upload: after contribution + authorization-policy persistence).
- Delivery is intentionally best-effort; subscriber failure is logged and can never make the caller mistake a failed side effect for a failed/committed primary operation.

### D2 — leaf-first ownership lookup

`getCommunityForCollaboraDocumentOrFail` is **deleted**. Its replacement starts from the selective document-owning relation:

1. probe `callout_contribution.collaboraDocumentId`, select only the owning callout's `calloutsSetId`;
2. if absent, probe `callout_framing.collaboraDocumentId` the same way;
3. delegate to the existing shallow `getLevelZeroSpaceIdForCalloutsSet` lookup.

Contribution path = two statements; framing fallback = at most three. Both leaf predicates are already backed by unique indexes (migrations `1777000000000-CreateCollaboraDocument`, `1777000000001-AddCollaboraDocumentToCalloutFraming`). Both not-found routes expose the static `EntityNotFoundException` message `Unable to find Space for CollaboraDocument`, with runtime identifiers in `details`.

### Site 4 — RabbitMQ contribution/view window consumer

Remains a direct, awaited service flow (it produces aggregate `writeActors`/`readonlyActors`/`alkemio` records, not single-actor lifecycle records). It adopts only the cheaper leaf-first lookup. Acknowledgement semantics are unchanged (`ack(context)` still precedes the integration service call).

### Single document fetch

`collaboraEditorUrl` now loads `profile` + backing `document` once; `getEditorUrl` accepts the loaded entity and issues the WOPI token without re-fetching the same `CollaboraDocument`.

## Analytics preserved

All five analytics record contracts remain active: `collaboraDocumentOpened`, `calloutCollaboraDocumentReplaced`, `calloutCollaboraDocumentUploaded`, `officeDocumentContribution`, `officeDocumentView`. The lifecycle subscriber emits exactly one structured INFO timing record per lookup attempt (success and failure).

## Release 71 residue to confirm removed

- [x] Temporary early returns / commented analytics blocks from PR #6354 removed (not carried forward).
- [x] Skipped unit-test assertions from the temp fix restored/replaced.
- [x] Old wide `getCommunityForCollaboraDocumentOrFail` lookup deleted; no Collabora two-call fetch pair remains.

## Domain impact

- Schema changes: **none**
- Migrations: **none**
- Deprecations: **none**
- RabbitMQ configuration changes: **none**
- Runtime dependency changes: **none**
- Public API / deployment components added: **none** (internal typed events + best-effort subscriber inside the existing module)

## Constitution

PR #6350 also proposes Constitution **2.0.0 → 3.0.0** (MAJOR): redefines Principle 4 (Explicit Data, Persistence & Event Flow) to make safe write-path ordering explicit, and adds Architecture Standard 6 (performance-sensitive ownership/attribution lookups must start at the most selective indexed leaf).

## Post-deploy acceptance

- **SC-001** — successful `CollaboraEditorUrl` p95 below **1 s** and no unexplained all-outcome transaction above 5 s. Zero successful samples ⇒ unverified.
- **SC-003** — first 20 structured lookup records (or all 1–19 within seven days) each below **100 ms**. Zero records ⇒ unverified.

Commands + evidence locations: `specs/110-collabora-editor-url-latency/quickstart.md`.

## Links

- Proper fix PR (this ticket): #6350 — feature `110-collabora-editor-url-latency` (merged 2026-08-13)
- Temporary fix (Release 71): #6354, base `release/71`
- Regression introduced by: #6187
- Original report: alkem-io/wopi-service#29
- Related tracking issue (temp fix): #6356
t: Collabora editor URL latency — proper fix (detach analytics + leaf-first ownership lookup)

## Summary

Every field on `LookupQueryResults` is declared `nullable: true` in the GraphQL schema, but its resolver calls a `...OrFail` service method that **throws `EntityNotFoundException`** instead of returning `null`. The schema advertises "this may be null"; the API actually returns a GraphQL error with no `data`.

**37 of 38** resolve-fields in `src/services/api/lookup/lookup.resolver.fields.ts` follow this pattern — `space`, `account`, `organization`, `user`, `conversation`, `roleSet`, `document`, `virtualContributor`, `post`, `room`, `whiteboard`, `callout`, and so on. There are 39 `@ResolveField`s, 38 `nullable: true` declarations, and 39 `...OrFail(` calls.

## Why it matters

A consumer reading the schema will reasonably write:

```ts
const { data } = await client.lookup({ id });
if (data.lookup.callout == null) { /* not found — handle gracefully */ }
```

That branch is unreachable. On a missing id the request resolves to `errors: [{ code: ENTITY_NOT_FOUND }]` with `data: null`, so the whole selection set is lost — including any sibling fields that resolved successfully. Clients must wrap every lookup in error handling that the schema gives them no reason to expect, and partial-success queries degrade to total failure.

It also generates avoidable test churn: an assertion written against the declared contract (`expect(lookup.callout).toBeNull()`) fails with `undefined`, and the test then gets "fixed" to match the implementation rather than the contract. This surfaced in test-suites while verifying the emoji-reactions coverage (test-suites#606), where `US4-AS3` asserted `toBeNull()` per the schema and had to be rewritten to assert the error instead.

## Reproduction

```graphql
query { lookup { callout(ID: "<any-nonexistent-uuid>") { id } } }
```

Actual:
```json
{ "errors": [ { "message": "Callout not found",
                "path": ["lookup", "callout"],
                "extensions": { "code": "ENTITY_NOT_FOUND" } } ] }
```
(no `data` key)

Expected, per the declared schema: `{ "data": { "lookup": { "callout": null } } }`

Source: `LookupResolverFields.callout` (`src/services/api/lookup/lookup.resolver.fields.ts`) → `CalloutService.getCalloutOrFail` (`src/domain/collaboration/callout/callout.service.ts`), which throws for any unknown id despite the field being nullable.

## Options

1. **Make the resolvers match the schema** — use the non-`OrFail` variants (or catch `EntityNotFoundException`) and return `null`. Correct per the declared contract, but a behavioural change for anyone currently relying on the error, so it needs a deprecation note in the release.
2. **Make the schema match the resolvers** — drop `nullable: true` and document that lookups throw. Honest and cheap, but loses the ability to express "not found" without failing the whole query, and still discards sibling fields.
3. Leave as-is and document the divergence prominently in the API docs.

Option 1 looks right for a `lookup` API whose purpose is "fetch this if it exists", but the call is yours — the blast radius is every consumer of `lookup.*`.

## Notes

Pre-existing and platform-wide; not a regression, and not caused by any feature in flight. Raised so it stops silently shaping test assertions.

t: lookup.* fields declare nullable but throw ENTITY_NOT_FOUND — schema/resolver contract mismatch (37 of 38 fields)
